essays.title: How Much Does an AI Agent Cost in India? (2026 Breakdown)
essays.excerpt: How much does an AI agent cost in India? Fixed-scope projects from ₹25,000, hourly ₹1,500, retainers ₹30,000-75,000/month. The full 2026 breakdown of what drives price.
essays.body:
If you are searching "how much does an AI agent cost in India", here is the direct answer from a working AI engineer in Ahmedabad: fixed-scope agent projects start from ₹25,000, typically delivered in 2 to 4 weeks; hourly work is ₹1,500; retainers run ₹30,000-75,000 per month for 10 to 25 hours with priority turnaround. Full-time arrangements are negotiable. Everything below explains what moves those numbers and how to read any quote you receive, including mine.

The numbers, up front

  • AI workflow automation: ₹15,000-35,000, fixed scope, usually days-to-weeks.
  • Website with lead capture: ₹10,000-20,000.
  • AI product or MVP (agent with tools, guardrails, deployment): ₹25,000-60,000+.
  • Hourly: ₹1,500 per hour, billed weekly against capped hours.
  • Retainer: ₹30,000-75,000 per month, 10 to 25 hours, priority turnaround.
  • Full-time: negotiable, discussed on a call.

Payment structure is 40% upfront and 60% on delivery. You get a fixed quote in writing before any work starts, two revision rounds are included, and the code lands in your repo and your cloud, not mine. A free 15-minute intro call is always the first step; there is no obligation to proceed after it. Full details live on the pricing page.

One cost nobody puts in the project price, because it is not mine to charge: model API usage is billed by the provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and so on) directly to you, usage-based. A lean agent might spend very little per month; a chatty multi-agent system spends more. An honest quote separates build cost from run cost, and so does mine.

What actually drives the price up or down

Integrations and auth

An agent that only reads a PDF is simple. An agent that must authenticate into your CRM, respect per-user permissions, write back records and trigger webhooks is a different product. Every external system adds contract design, error handling, token management and testing. This is usually the single biggest swing factor after scope.

Data quality

Clean, structured data makes everything cheaper. Messy scans, duplicated records, inconsistent field names and tribal knowledge in someone's head all add cleaning and discovery work before the agent builds anything. If your data is rough, part of the budget goes to making it usable, and that is still cheaper than a model trained to cope with chaos.

Eval and verification surface

How much of the system must be provably correct, and how do we check it? An agent drafting marketing copy tolerates different failure rates than one issuing refunds. Verification gates, regression suites and tenant-scoping guards cost engineering time, and they are the difference between a demo and a system your customers never notice failing. Skipping them does not make the project cheaper; it makes the failure expensive.

Compliance and review requirements

Regulated data, audit logs, approval workflows or legal review loops all add scope. None of this is exotic, but it multiplies the test matrix and the documentation. Say it up front so it is priced honestly instead of discovered mid-build.

Scope creep

The ₹25,000 quote covers the written scope and two revision rounds. "While you are here, can it also..." is how fixed scope quietly becomes hourly scope. Changes are welcome; they get re-quoted in writing before they get built, so you never see a surprise invoice.

Fixed-scope vs hourly vs retainer: when each makes sense

Fixed-scope is right when the task and definition of done are nameable: an automation, a specific agent, an MVP. You know the maximum cost in advance, delivery is typically 2 to 4 weeks, and the 40/60 split keeps both sides accountable. This is the right starting point for almost every first engagement.

Hourly fits open-ended or exploratory work: audits, rescue of a half-finished agent, spike investigations where the outcome genuinely cannot be scoped yet. Capped hours and weekly billing keep it controlled.

Retainer is for after launch: model upgrades, prompt and eval maintenance, new integrations, on-call-ish support, priority turnaround on fixes. ₹30,000-75,000 per month depending on volume. Think of it as keeping the system honest as your business changes, not as paying for idle capacity.

What "from ₹25,000" includes, and what it does not

Included, at the starting band: architecture and a written plan, the build itself, deployment to your cloud, a handoff document, two revision rounds, and the repo with the code. You own all of it from day one.

Not included, at any band: model API bills (usage-based, billed by the provider to you), third-party SaaS subscriptions the agent integrates with, and hosting or infrastructure costs for your cloud account. Also not included: unlimited revisions, scope beyond the written document, and guaranteed business outcomes, because no honest engineer can promise those. What you do get is a working system, the runbook to operate it, and the truth about its limits.

How to evaluate any AI agent quote

Use this checklist on mine and everyone else's:

  1. Written scope. Task, inputs, outputs, explicit exclusions. No document, no deal.
  2. Definition of done. What acceptance looks like, in testable terms, not "the agent works well".
  3. What happens when the agent is wrong. Fallback path, human escalation, and whether the system degrades gracefully below a confidence threshold.
  4. Who owns the code and the cloud resources. It should be you, unambiguously, from the first commit.
  5. What the evals show. Ask to see the test set and the results. If the vendor has never built an eval set, they are selling demos.
  6. Delivery timeline and payment terms in writing. Two to four weeks is typical for a fixed-scope pilot; anything vague is a red flag.

A worked example, kept generic

Two common shapes, no invented case studies:

Shape one: the weekly manual task. Every Friday someone exports data, reformats it, pastes it into a spreadsheet and emails it to five stakeholders. The fix is a workflow automation: scheduled pull, deterministic transform where possible, model only for the judgment step (say, summarizing exceptions), send and log. This is the ₹15,000-35,000 band. Delivery is measured in weeks, not months, and the ROI is simply the returned hours plus near-eliminated copy-paste errors.

Shape two: the customer-facing agent. An agent that answers product questions from your docs, cites sources, escalates refunds above a limit to a human, and logs every interaction tenant-safely. That needs retrieval, an eval set of real questions, a confidence/faithfulness gate that says "I don't know" below threshold, observability and a deployment with monitoring. That is the ₹25,000+ band, starting at the lower end only if your docs and data are already in decent shape. It is also why model API usage, priced per token, lands on you as the system handles real volume.

Both shapes start the same way: a free 15-minute call, a written scope, a fixed quote. The call is where we figure out which shape you actually have, and sometimes the honest answer is a script, not an agent.

After delivery: what ownership and maintenance look like

Delivery is not the end of the cost story, and pretending otherwise sets you up for the second invoice that was never discussed. An agent in production touches model providers, your data and your customers, and all three change. Budget for light, recurring attention: prompt and eval maintenance as models update, occasional integration fixes when third-party APIs change, and a quarterly review of the eval set so it reflects current reality. This can be an hourly arrangement or a retainer; the point is that someone is watching the gates, not that you are paying for idle time. If you inherited the repo and the handoff doc, you can also bring this in-house, which is exactly why the code goes to your repo rather than mine.

How to start

Book a free 15-minute intro call via the contact page or kunjkshah05@gmail.com. Bring the workflow as it runs today and the cost of doing nothing. Within a day of the call you get a written scope and a fixed quote; if it is not a fit, you keep the scoping document anyway. No obligation, no retainer required to begin, and no surprises after delivery.

essays.title: AI Agent Development Guide: From Brief to Production
essays.excerpt: How to plan, build and ship an AI agent that survives production: scope, tool contracts, evals, verification gates and the fixed-scope pilot that de-risks it all.
essays.body:
If you are planning an AI agent project, the honest starting point is this: an agent is not a model with a prompt. It is a small software system with tools, state, verification and a handover plan, wrapped around a model that will sometimes be wrong. The projects that ship treat the model as one component among several. The projects that stall treat it as the whole product.

I am Kunj Shah, an AI engineer in Ahmedabad. I have shipped 17+ systems and merged 60+ PRs across 24 external repositories. This guide is how I scope, build and verify agent work for clients and for my own products. It is written for a founder or engineering lead deciding whether to commission an agent, and for the engineer who will have to maintain it afterwards.

What an agent project actually consists of

Every agent engagement I have taken on decomposes into five parts. If a proposal skips one of them, the proposal is incomplete, not lean.

  • Scope. One narrow task with a written definition of done. "Handle customer support" is not scope. "Draft a first response to billing disputes using our policy docs, escalate anything with a refund over the limit" is scope.
  • Tools. Typed contracts for every action the agent may take: search, read, write, call API, send message. Each tool needs an input schema, an error model and a permission boundary.
  • State. What the agent remembers between steps and between sessions, and where that lives. For anything multi-step, this usually means a checkpointed graph, not a growing string in a prompt.
  • Verification. An independent check that the agent's claimed output is actually correct. This is the part most projects skip, and the part that decides whether you can trust the system.
  • Handover. Code in your repo, your cloud, a short handoff doc, and a rollback story. An agent you cannot inspect is an agent you cannot operate.

The build order that works

I build in this order, and I push back on clients who want to reorder it. Each step produces an artifact the next step depends on.

1. Narrow the task until it is boring

The first milestone of any agent project should be unglamorous. Pick the single highest-frequency, lowest-risk slice of the workflow. If the workflow is reviewing pull requests, start with dependency-bump PRs, not architecture changes. Breadth comes later; correctness comes first.

2. Write tool contracts before prompts

For each tool: name, purpose, parameters, return shape, failure modes, and what the agent must do when the tool fails. Contracts written first expose the impossible parts of the task early. They also make the agent testable without the model in the loop, because you can fake the tools and check the wiring.

3. Model the flow as an explicit state machine

Implicit control flow is where agent projects rot. Make the states and transitions explicit: plan, act, verify, retry, escalate. Graph-first orchestration (I use LangGraph in every production system I ship) forces you to name every edge, including the failure edges, and gives you checkpointing and human-in-the-loop interrupts for free. More on that in the EngineerOS case study.

4. Build the eval set before the agent is finished

Collect real inputs and the correct outputs, then fix them as a regression suite. Twenty questions is enough to start. EngineerOS runs a 20-question retrieval test in CI that fails the build if recall drops below its floor. That single gate has caught regressions that manual spot-checking missed, because people get tired and CI does not.

5. Add a verification gate the agent cannot talk its way past

This is the rule I learned the hard way. In OnRamp, a 9-step pipeline ingests a shallow clone, builds an AST graph across 20+ languages (Python ast plus tree-sitter), renders a D3 visualization, routes analysis to models, classifies issues by difficulty and assigns them by role, assigns tasks load-aware (fewest active non-terminal tasks, round-robin tie-break), opens one PR per issue, then validates and reviews. Validation re-parses the PR head and diffs the graph against base for broken edges and cycles, with bounded retries and a structured SENIOR_REVIEW.md. The lesson generalizes: a generated PR only counts once the validator re-parses it and diffs the graph, because the agent's own summary is the thing you cannot trust. Verification must read the world's state, not the agent's claims about the world.

6. Deploy behind a human-in-the-loop checkpoint

Ship the agent in propose-then-approve mode first. Log every decision, measure acceptance rates, and only then consider auto-approving the slices where the human never overrode the agent. This is also your onboarding path for the team that will operate it.

Cost and latency control are architecture, not tuning

Agents amplify model costs by making many calls per task, so cost control belongs in the design, not in a spreadsheet after launch. Two levers do most of the work.

The first is routing. Not every step in a pipeline needs a frontier model. OnRamp routes free-tier models first (OpenRouter, Gemini, Groq, NVIDIA) and keeps DeepSeek, Qwen, Zhipu, Moonshot, Mistral, OpenAI, Anthropic, HuggingFace and Ollama behind that wall. The practical rule: classify the difficulty of each sub-task, send the easy 80% to cheap or free models, and reserve expensive models for the steps where quality measurably changes the outcome. Model routing is a cost-control problem before it is a capability problem.

The second is caching. Exact-hash caching catches repeated identical calls; semantic caching at 0.85 similarity catches near-duplicates with different wording. Both are cheap to add and they compound, because agent workloads revisit the same sub-problems constantly. If you do neither, your agent will quietly cost far more to run than it needs to. The exact multiple depends on your workload, so measure your own cache hit rate; what is knowable is that uncached agent loops are the most common silent budget leak in production.

Latency follows the same logic. EngineerOS, a LangGraph multi-agent system with checkpointing and semantic search (HNSW), holds p95 retrieval under 200ms, and the end-to-end experience survives because retrieval is not the bottleneck most teams assume it to be. Measure each span before optimizing it. Streaming partial results to the UI also matters more than raw model speed for perceived latency, since users tolerate a visibly working agent far better than a frozen one.

What an agent is not

Worth saying plainly, because it saves clients money: not every automation wants an agent. If the task is fully deterministic, a workflow with no model in it is cheaper, faster and more reliable. If the corpus fits in the context window, retrieval infrastructure is overkill. If the answer requires aggregating a million rows, that is a database query, not a language task. An agent earns its complexity when the task has unstructured inputs, judgment calls, or tool use that varies per case, and no fixed script covers the variation.

During the intro call I will tell you which of these buckets your problem falls into. Sometimes the honest answer is "buy a script, not an agent", and you will get that answer before you have spent anything.

Where agent projects fail

Four failure modes account for almost every agent project I have been called in to rescue.

No evals, or evals that test nothing real

If you cannot say "on last month's 50 real cases, the agent handled 41 correctly", you do not have an agent, you have a demo. Evals must use real historical inputs, not synthetic ones written by the person who built the prompt. Synthetic evals flatter the system.

Self-reported success

Walkcast made this failure visible. A published lab run had 3 of 4 agent success claims turn out to be false; the harness flagged all three by checking the application's real state instead of the agent's claim. Failed runs become reproducible regression fixtures that gate releases in CI (129 test cases there). Whenever I see an agent whose only source of truth is its own final message, I expect the success rate to be fiction.

Provider lock-in

OnRamp routes free-tier models first (OpenRouter, Gemini, Groq, NVIDIA) and keeps DeepSeek, Qwen, Zhipu, Moonshot, Mistral, OpenAI, Anthropic, HuggingFace and Ollama behind that, with Redis exact plus semantic caching. That routing is a cost-control problem before it is a capability problem. If your agent cannot swap providers, every price change and every outage becomes a re-architecture. Keep the model behind an interface, keep prompts provider-agnostic where possible, and cache aggressively.

Unbounded scope

Scope creep kills agents faster than bad models do. "While you are in there, can it also..." is how a 3-week pilot becomes a 9-month program. The fix is a written scope with an explicit not-included list, and a change-request process that re-prices rather than absorbs.

How to de-risk: the fixed-scope pilot

Every agent project I take on starts with a fixed-scope pilot, and I recommend you demand this from anyone you hire, not just from me.

  • Written scope. A one to two page document: task, inputs, outputs, definition of done, explicit exclusions.
  • Fixed price, fixed time. Typically 2 to 4 weeks. You know the cost before the first commit.
  • Code in your repo and your cloud. You own the artifact from day one. If the engagement ends, you keep everything.
  • A gate before scale-up. The pilot ends with an honest review against the eval set. Scale-up is a separate decision, made on evidence, not on enthusiasm.

Estate360 shows what the verification layer looks like in a tenant-facing system: an agentic answer loop with confidence 0.65 and faithfulness 0.8 gates, every query tenant-scoped and enforced by a CI guard. Below the gate, the system says it does not know instead of guessing. That behavior is a feature worth paying for, because the alternative is plausible wrong answers delivered with confidence.

Fixed pricing also aligns incentives. I take the risk on my own estimates, you get a known number, and the 40/60 payment split (40% upfront, 60% on delivery) keeps both sides honest.

A realistic definition of production

"Production" for an agent means all of the following are true: the eval suite runs in CI and passes its floor; the verification gate reads external state, not agent claims; failures degrade to a safe path (human handoff or "I don't know"); you have logs and metrics for latency, cost and acceptance rate; and a named human owns the runbook. If any of these is missing, you are piloting, which is fine, as long as everyone calls it that.

Frequently asked questions before you commission

Do I need a dedicated AI engineer on staff?

For a pilot, no. For a portfolio of agent systems, eventually yes, or a retainer with someone who maintains them. Either way, insist that documentation and code land with you, so the dependency is on knowledge transfer, not on a single vendor.

Which model should the agent use?

Whichever the eval set proves out, behind an interface so you can swap it. I use free-tier-first routing for cost and escalate to paid frontier models only where evals show a real quality delta. Anyone who names one model for every task has not run the evals.

What if the agent is wrong?

The verification gate catches what it can, and the safe fallback catches the rest: human escalation or an honest "I don't know". Estate360 degrades below its confidence 0.65 and faithfulness 0.8 gates rather than guess. Plan for wrongness; it is a design input, not an exception.

What should I prepare before the call?

Bring the workflow as it happens today: the inputs, the people, the current failure rate, and the cost of each failure. Twenty minutes of that conversation tells us both whether an agent is viable, and what the pilot would prove.

How to start

If you are deciding whether to commission an agent, start with a free 15-minute intro call. We will map your workflow, name the narrowest viable slice, and I will send a fixed quote in writing within a day of the call. No retainer is required to start, and there is no obligation to proceed. Pricing starts at ₹25,000 for fixed-scope work; details are on the pricing page. Reach out via the contact page or kunjkshah05@gmail.com, and we will tell you honestly whether an agent is even the right tool for your problem. Sometimes it is not, and I would rather say that on the call than after you have paid.

essays.title: Building AI Agents for the Web: CAPTCHAs, Logins and Layout Drift
essays.excerpt: Building AI agents for the web? The honest guide to CAPTCHAs, login walls and layout drift: authorized paths only, human-in-the-loop at irreversible steps, verified state.
essays.body:
What browser agents are actually like in production

In a demo, a browser agent is magic: it opens a page, reads the DOM, clicks around and completes the task while you watch. In production it is closer to a night-shift worker with a flickering flashlight. It can browse websites, fill forms and perform multi-step tasks, and the hard part is never the clicking. The hard part is reliability, security and authorization.

Every navigation is a state transition that can fail: the page loads halfway, a modal you did not expect appears, the session expires mid-flow, the button you were aiming at moved. An agent that does not treat each transition as fallible is not an automation; it is a liability with a pleasant voice. The rest of this essay covers the three walls I plan around, the working principles that keep browser agents honest, and the line I will not cross.

It is worth separating two kinds of browser automation before going further. Internal tools you own, such as your own admin panel or an internal dashboard, are the healthy kind: you control the interface, you can pin the layout and you can add stable test IDs as you go. Third-party websites are the fragile kind: the interface is someone else's moving target, and every assumption your agent makes about it is rented, not owned.

Wall one: CAPTCHAs

CAPTCHAs and other anti-bot measures exist to stop exactly what agents do. That is their purpose, not an inconvenience to be optimized away. The honest engineering position: I do not defeat anti-bot systems, and I will not build tooling whose business value depends on evading them.

When a CAPTCHA appears mid-task, the correct behavior is to stop and escalate to the human, not to solve it covertly. A CAPTCHA is the application telling you, in the application's own words, that this action requires a human judgment. Treating that signal as an obstacle to route around is not engineering; it is unauthorized access with extra steps.

If a flow requires beating a CAPTCHA to complete, the flow is not automatable on my watch. The alternatives are always legitimate paths: official APIs, test accounts, agreed partner access, or a human completing that one step while the agent handles everything around it. The agent pauses at the wall and hands over the keys rather than picking the lock.

In practice the human-in-the-loop pattern feels almost boring, which is the point. The agent fills the form, attaches the documents, navigates to the confirmation screen, then stops and pings a person: "ready to submit, confirm?" The person glances, clicks, done. You keep the speed of automation on the mechanical work and the judgment of a human on the steps that are not.

Wall two: logins and MFA

Login walls and multi-factor authentication are the second wall, and they deserve the same honesty. Credentials should not be pasted into prompts, logged in traces or stored in plaintext fixtures. The sane pattern is a scoped session: a dedicated test account or service identity, least-privilege access, MFA handled by the human or by an authenticator the organization controls, and secrets in a vault, never in the repository.

Where MFA is mandatory, the agent stops at the challenge and the human completes it. That is not a failure of automation; it is the division of labour that keeps the organization safe. The agent does the repetitive work, the human does the steps that carry legal and security weight. If the login itself is the product, such as a consumer account only its owner can access, the browser agent is the wrong tool and no amount of engineering changes that.

Wall three: layout drift

Layout drift is the quiet killer. A redesigned page silently breaks a selector-driven agent, and the agent, being eager to please, clicks the nearest plausible element instead of the right one. On a payments page, "nearest plausible" is how money moves to the wrong place. Selector drift is not a cosmetic annoyance; it is a correctness bug that only shows up in production, usually at the worst time.

Visual and structural changes land without notice because the page is not under your version control. The only safe posture is to assume the interface will change and to design detection, escalation and rollback around that assumption. The next two sections cover how.

The authorized-path principle

My rule for browser automation is simple: automate only what you are authorized to automate, through paths the owner of the system has agreed to. In practice that means, in order of preference:

  1. Official APIs first. If the service offers an API, use it. APIs are stable contracts with versioning; UIs are neither.
  2. Official automation programs. Many platforms publish sanctioned automation or partner programs. Use them, even if the paperwork is boring.
  3. Your own test environments. Staging and QA instances exist precisely so robots and humans can break things safely before customers see anything.
  4. Agreed partner access. If you have a commercial relationship with the platform, negotiate API or test-account access rather than scraping around the front door.
  5. Human-in-the-loop at irreversible steps. Purchases, sends, deletes, publishes: the agent prepares, the human confirms. One click, one accountable human.
  6. Deterministic fallbacks. When the model is unsure, the system falls back to a rules-based path or pauses for a human, rather than improvising against a live interface.

This ordering is deliberate. Every step down the list trades away reliability, auditability or legal safety, and the trade is rarely worth it for tasks with a first-class interface.

Layout drift and how to detect it early

Drift detection is a monitoring problem, not a prompt-engineering problem. The playbook I use, in rough order of deployment:

  • Pre-flight checks. Before the task starts, verify the expected landmarks: page title, key selectors, account context, environment banner. If the environment changed, fail loudly before any action is taken.
  • State verification after every step. Confirm the outcome from application state, not from the agent's summary. This is the Walkcast approach, documented at kunjshah.in/projects/walkcast, and it applies to web flows exactly as it does to any other agent action.
  • Alert on drift, never silently improvise. A moved button should page a human, not trigger a creative click. Improvisation on an unrecognized screen is how agents send the wrong email to the wrong list.
  • Replay fixtures per flow. Each critical flow gets a recorded fixture that replays in CI, so drift is caught before the next scheduled run, not after the wrong button gets clicked across the scheduled runs.

Done together, these turn drift from a silent production incident into a loud, boring pre-flight failure. Boring is the goal.

Two operational details complete the picture. First, session expiry is a normal event, not an exception: the flow must detect a logged-out state and either re-authenticate through the approved path or pause and escalate, never wander around a login page retrying. Second, scheduled runs should happen during off-peak hours where possible, both to respect the platform and to keep a human available when the human-in-the-loop step fires.

What I will and won't build

I will not build: CAPTCHA circumvention, credential stuffing, unauthorized scraping past an explicit denial, or any flow whose authorization is ambiguous. If the site says no, the answer is no. No architecture, prompt or "but everyone does it" changes that.

I will build: automations on owned flows, internal tools where you are the operator, partner integrations backed by written agreement, and human-in-the-loop pipelines where every irreversible step stops for confirmation. If you want authorized automation for your own systems, reach out at kunjshah.in/contact and we will scope it honestly.

When a browser agent is the wrong tool

Two cases, both common. First, a documented API exists: use it, because APIs do not have layouts, do not drift at 2 AM and come with real error codes. A browser agent driving a UI that has an official API behind it is complexity you chose on purpose. Second, the task needs no UI at all: if the work is data in, decision, data out, a script or a scheduled job will outlive any selector-based approach.

If neither case applies and the flow is yours, a browser agent can be the right tool, wrapped in pre-flight checks, state verification, drift alerting and a human at the irreversible steps. That is the whole discipline: authorized paths, verified state, and a person accountable at the steps that cannot be undone.

essays.title: LangGraph vs CrewAI: Which Agent Framework Should You Use?
essays.excerpt: LangGraph vs CrewAI compared honestly: who owns the control flow, graph-first state and checkpointing vs the role-based crew metaphor, and how to choose.
essays.body:
If you are choosing between LangGraph and CrewAI, the real question is not which framework is better. It is who owns the control flow: you, or the framework. That one decision, made consciously, resolves most of the confusion in this debate. Everything else, syntax, abstractions, docs, is downstream of it.

I build and ship agent systems for clients and my own products, and every production system on this site runs LangGraph. CrewAI is a capable tool with real strengths, and this comparison tries to be fair to both. No invented stars, no benchmark theater; just the trade-offs I see when the code has to survive contact with production.

The real question you are answering when you choose

An agent framework is a claim about where the hard part lives. In LangGraph, the hard part is your state machine: nodes, edges, state schema, interrupts. In CrewAI, the hard part is the organization: roles, goals, tasks, and the process that sequences them. If your risk is "the flow must never do X", you want explicit control of edges. If your risk is "we need five plausible role-shaped drafts by Friday", you want the crew metaphor to do the scaffolding.

Neither framework removes the need for evals, a verification gate and cost control. They only change how much structure you assemble by hand.

LangGraph: graph-first, explicit state, enforceable invariants

LangGraph models the agent as a graph over a typed state object. You declare the nodes (plan, retrieve, act, verify), the edges (including conditional and failure edges), and the state schema that flows through them. What you get in return:

  • Explicit, deterministic edges. Every transition is named and inspectable. When a run misbehaves, the path it took is visible in the trace, not buried in a prompt history.
  • Checkpointing. State can be persisted at step boundaries, which enables resume, replay, audit and human-in-the-loop approval before irreversible actions.
  • Interrupts for human-in-loop. You can pause the graph at any node, get a human decision, and resume with the prior state intact. This is the cleanest primitive for approving risky actions.
  • Streaming and observability. Token and state-step streaming maps cleanly to UIs, and the graph structure makes tracing legible for postmortems.
  • Invariants you can enforce. If the flow must verify before writing, or tenant-scope every query, that is an edge you can require, not a hope you bake into a prompt.

Two shipped systems on this site use it. The resumemaster-ai routing gateway sits in front of an LLM and classifies each request by complexity, routing cheap tasks to cheaper models; it cut API spend by 65% with a complexity classifier, human-in-loop review, and under 200ms of added latency. The archmind-research-agent runs a planner, search, extract and write pipeline as an explicit graph, which is what makes multi-step research runs inspectable instead of magical.

The costs are real. LangGraph has a steeper learning curve. You write more boilerplate: state schemas, node functions, edge logic. And you own every edge case, because the framework will not invent your failure paths for you. Teams that want a demo by tomorrow will bounce off it; teams that need the flow to be provably correct will not go back.

CrewAI: the role-based crew metaphor

CrewAI structures an agent system as a crew of role-played agents: a researcher, a writer, an editor, each with a goal and a task list, orchestrated by a process (sequential or hierarchical). For the right shape of problem it is genuinely fast scaffolding.

Where it shines:

  • Rapid prototyping. Role, goal, task, run. Internal prototypes and content or research workflows get to a convincing demo quickly.
  • Role-based decomposition. When the problem genuinely decomposes into hats people wear (analyst, reviewer, summarizer), the metaphor matches how stakeholders think, which makes demos and sign-off easier.
  • Hierarchical processes. A manager agent can delegate and review, which maps well to editorial-style workflows.
  • Lower ceremony. Less explicit graph code means faster iteration early, when requirements are still fluid.

The trade-offs appear when requirements get specific. Edge-level control and state shape are less granular than LangGraph's; enforcing hard invariants (verify-before-write, tenant isolation, bounded retries) is harder to express and harder to audit. You end up fighting the framework's abstractions exactly when the business needs guarantees. Hierarchical delegation can also meander: more agents, more calls, more places for the plan to drift, unless you constrain the process tightly.

None of this makes CrewAI wrong. It makes it a prototyping-and-workflow tool first, and a control plane second.

The decision table

SituationBetter fitWhy
Production flow with hard invariants (verify before write, tenant scoping)LangGraphEdges and state are explicit; invariants live in the graph, not the prompt
Human-in-the-loop approval before irreversible actionsLangGraphInterrupts and checkpointing are first-class primitives
Fast role-based prototype or content/research workflowCrewAICrew metaphor scaffolds quickly with minimal ceremony
Internal tool where the cost of a wrong step is lowCrewAISpeed of iteration outweighs edge-level control
Long-lived system with audit and compliance needsLangGraphReplayable state and legible traces support postmortems and review
Either framework, any stakesYour evals and router matter moreFramework choice does not fix retrieval, verification or cost routing

A decision heuristic I use: if you can write the flow as a numbered list with "if this fails, stop" in it, that flow wants LangGraph. If you can describe it as "the analyst researches, the writer drafts, the editor polishes", it wants CrewAI, until the day it needs a hard guarantee, at which point you port the invariant into a graph.

Observability and debugging day two

The first demo is easy; day two is when the frameworks diverge in practice. With LangGraph, a bad run is a trace of node transitions over typed state, so you can replay the exact path, inspect what the retriever returned, and see which conditional edge fired. With CrewAI, the trace centers on tasks and delegations, which is legible for editorial review but coarser when you need to prove why a specific tool call happened. In both cases you should wire the same hygiene: structured logs, per-step latency and cost, and a store of full traces for sampled runs. If your debugging workflow is "paste the prompt into chat and ask the model why it failed", the framework is not the problem, but neither will it save you.

Migrating between the two

Teams often prototype in CrewAI and graduate hot paths to LangGraph. The migration is mostly mechanical: map each crew role to a node or subgraph, move task descriptions into node prompts, and lift shared memory into the typed state schema. The genuinely hard part is discovering the hidden invariants the prototype was silently violating, which is why the migration is a good moment to write the eval set if you skipped it. Going the other direction, LangGraph to CrewAI, is rare and usually a sign that the original requirements were over-engineered.

What actually predicts success regardless of framework

After enough builds, the pattern is unmistakable: the teams that succeed are not the ones with the shinier abstraction; they are the ones with the unglamorous disciplines.

  1. Evals on real cases. A fixed set of historical inputs with verified-correct outputs, run in CI, failing the build below a floor. No eval suite means no idea whether you are improving or regressing.
  2. A verification gate the agent cannot talk past. Check real system state: re-parse the PR, diff the graph, validate the tenant. The agent's own summary is not evidence.
  3. Cost routing. Classify request complexity and route to the cheapest adequate model, with caching on top. This is where budgets actually get saved.
  4. Explicit failure paths. Bounded retries, safe degradation, human escalation. Systems that only model the happy path fail in production in front of customers.
  5. Human-in-loop where it counts. Approval gates on irreversible or high-blast-radius actions, removed gradually as measured trust grows.

LangGraph makes these disciplines easier to express; CrewAI can host them too, with more manual wiring. Neither ships them for you.

My honest recommendation

Default to LangGraph for anything customer-facing, money-moving or multi-tenant, because invariants and auditability are not negotiable there. Reach for CrewAI for internal prototypes and role-shaped content workflows where speed beats control, with a plan to revisit if the stakes rise. And if you are unsure, the cheapest resolution is not another comparison post; it is a one-week spike with a fixed eval set, which will tell you empirically which framework your team can operate well.

If you want help making that call for your specific workflow, contact me; the first conversation is free and I will tell you plainly whether you need a framework at all.

essays.title: RAG Implementation Best Practices: Hybrid Search, Re-ranking and CI-Gated Recall
essays.excerpt: RAG implementation best practices for production: hybrid search, re-ranking, structure-aware chunking, CI-gated recall and faithfulness checks that stop guessing.
essays.body:
If you are searching for RAG implementation best practices, here is the short version: retrieval quality decides whether the system works, not which model sits on top. Everything else in this guide, chunking, hybrid search, re-ranking, caching, faithfulness gates, exists to make the right context reach the model reliably, and to make failures loud instead of silent.

I build retrieval systems for client work and for my own products. Two systems on this site carry the load of these lessons: Estate360, an agentic answer loop for real-estate workflows with confidence and faithfulness gates, and EngineerOS, a LangGraph multi-agent system whose retrieval test gates CI. This guide is what I would tell any team about to ship RAG to real users.

Retrieval quality matters more than model choice

Teams routinely spend weeks swapping models and days on retrieval. That is backwards. A frontier model with the wrong three chunks in context produces a confident wrong answer; a mid-tier model with the right three chunks produces a usable one. Before you touch the model, measure recall: does the context you retrieve actually contain the answer, and does it rank it near the top? If retrieval is broken, no model swap will save you, and if retrieval is good, model choice becomes a cost and latency decision rather than a correctness one.

Chunking: structure-aware, not character-count

Naive fixed-size chunking splits sentences in half and separates answers from the headings that define them. Structure-aware chunking splits on the document's own skeleton: headings, sections, list boundaries, table rows. Keep the section path as metadata on every chunk; it is cheap to store and it pays for itself in citation quality and in filtering.

As a documented working point, I use roughly 380-word chunks with a 50-word overlap. That is a starting position, not a law. The overlap exists so that an answer straddling a boundary is still retrievable whole. What matters is that you pick a point, document it, and re-measure when you change it, because every chunking decision ripples into your index, your embeddings and your evals.

Hybrid search and re-ranking

Pure vector search under-recalls exact identifiers. Product codes, ticket IDs, error strings, proper nouns, version numbers: embeddings blur these, because semantic similarity was never designed to respect an exact string. Keyword search (BM25 or Postgres full-text) nails them and misses paraphrase. You need both.

The architecture that works in production is: run vector and keyword retrieval in parallel, fuse the ranked lists (reciprocal rank fusion is the simple, robust option), then re-rank the fused candidates with a cross-encoder or a small model before stuffing context. Re-ranking is where most of the precision gain lives, because fusion alone leaves ordering noisy. In Postgres, this maps to pgvector for the dense side and full-text search with GIN indexes for the sparse side, fused in SQL or in application code. Keep the two indexes consistent with the same source-of-truth table.

Embeddings: comparable only within one model

Embeddings from different models live in different spaces. A vector from model A is meaningless to model B, even at the same dimensionality. The practical consequences: pin the embedding model in your config, version it, and record it with the index. If you switch embedders, you must re-embed and rebuild the index; there is no migration shortcut. Budget reindex time into any plan that includes "we might upgrade the embedding model later", which is most plans. Mixed-index querying across two embedders returns garbage quietly, which is worse than an error.

Evaluate with a fixed set of real questions, in CI

RAG degrades silently. A prompt tweak, a chunking change, an embedding bump, a new parser: any of these can drop recall without a single user-visible error until the complaints arrive. The fix is boring and effective: fix a set of real questions with known-good answers (20 is a workable start), run it in CI, and fail the build below a recall floor.

EngineerOS does exactly this. Its 20-question retrieval test fails the build if recall drops below its floor. That gate is the reason retrieval changes ship with confidence instead of with crossed fingers. Build the question set from actual support tickets, actual sales questions, actual internal docs queries. Synthetic questions written by the engineer who built the prompt will flatter the system every time. Include hard cases: ambiguous phrasing, identifiers, multi-hop questions, and questions that have no answer in the corpus.

Measure faithfulness, not just retrieval

Recall tells you the answer was in the context. Faithfulness tells you the model actually used it instead of freelancing. Both are necessary; only one is commonly measured. Estate360 gates at 0.8 faithfulness and 0.65 confidence, and below those gates it degrades to "I don't know" instead of guessing. That is the correct failure mode for a tenant-facing system, where a confident wrong answer about a lease or a listing can cost real money. Estate360 also scopes every query to the tenant, and that scoping is enforced by a CI guard, not by developer discipline, which is the only kind of enforcement that survives staff turnover.

Faithfulness is scored by an evaluator model against the retrieved context: does every claim in the answer trace to a chunk, or does it wander? Run it on your fixed question set in CI alongside recall. When faithfulness drops, do not just tweak the prompt; check whether the retrieved chunks actually support the question, because low faithfulness is often a retrieval problem wearing a generation costume.

Cache aggressively: exact and semantic

RAG workloads are repetitive. Cache at two levels: an exact-match cache keyed on a hash of the normalized query plus corpus version, and a semantic cache that matches near-duplicate queries at 0.85 similarity. The second catches the same question asked fifty ways. Invalidate both caches on corpus update and on embedder change. Estate360 and OnRamp both use exact plus semantic caching; it is the cheapest latency and cost win available, and it shrinks provider bills without touching quality. Measure hit rates, and remember that a stale cache serving outdated answers is worse than no cache at all, so tie cache lifetime to corpus freshness requirements.

Citations are first-class UI, not debug output

If the user cannot see which chunks produced the answer, they cannot verify it, and trust never forms. Render citations inline, link them to the source document at the right section, and make them clickable. Citations also give you free debugging: when a user reports a wrong answer, the citation trail shows whether retrieval or generation failed. Design them into the interface from the first mock, not as an afterthought bolted on after launch. Small details compound: show the document title and section, highlight the quoted span, and keep the citation count honest rather than dumping every retrieved chunk at the bottom.

Multi-format sources

Real corpora are not markdown. You will face PDFs with tables, DOCX with tracked changes, scanned images, audio call recordings, video walkthroughs. The parser layer decides your ceiling. Plan for a parser per format: text extraction with layout awareness for PDFs, structural parsing for DOCX, OCR or vision models for images, speech-to-text for audio, and frame sampling plus transcription for video. Normalize everything into the same chunk schema with source metadata (format, page, timestamp, author), so downstream stages never care where the content came from. Test parsers on ugly real files, not on the clean samples vendors show in demos. A parser that silently drops tables will cap your recall no matter how good your embeddings are.

Degrade gracefully without API keys

Development, CI and demos should not depend on live providers. Wire deterministic mocks behind the same interfaces: a fake LLM that returns templated answers from provided context, a deterministic embedder, a stub reranker. CI runs entirely on mocks plus the fixed question set's retrieval assertions, so builds never flake on provider outages or rate limits. When a real key is present, the same code paths run live. This pattern also makes onboarding new engineers painless: clone, run tests, no secrets required.

pgvector specifics worth knowing

If Postgres is your store, pgvector keeps the whole stack in one database, which simplifies backups, tenancy and transactional consistency. Create the embedding table with the tenant or namespace column you will filter on, and make that filter part of every query path, enforced in one shared function rather than copied per call site. For the keyword side, add a tsvector column with a GIN index and keep it updated with a trigger or during ingestion. Reciprocal rank fusion across the two result sets is a few lines of SQL or application code. One caveat: vector index choice (HNSW versus IVFFlat) trades build time, memory and recall; benchmark on your own corpus rather than trusting defaults, and revisit the choice whenever the corpus grows materially.

Common pitfalls I keep seeing

  • Embedding everything, citing nothing. Retrieval without citation plumbing gives you no way to debug or audit answers.
  • One index, forever. Corpora grow; indexes built on 10,000 chunks behave differently at 500,000. Re-measure recall on the fixed question set as the corpus scales.
  • Ignoring ingestion failures. A PDF that parsed to nothing does not error loudly; it just silently shrinks your effective corpus. Log and alert on per-file chunk counts.
  • Prompt tuning instead of retrieval tuning. When the answer is wrong, check the retrieved context first. Most "hallucinations" in RAG are retrieval gaps.
  • No corpus versioning. Cache keys, embeddings and eval results are all meaningless without knowing which corpus snapshot produced them.

Where RAG is the wrong tool

  • The corpus fits in context. If the whole knowledge base is a 20-page policy doc, put it in the prompt with caching and skip the retrieval stack. You will spend less engineering time and get better answers.
  • The data changes hourly. If answers must reflect stock levels or live order status, retrieval over a stale index is the wrong abstraction. Query the live system behind a tool and let the model call it.
  • The answer needs aggregation, not retrieval. "What was our average resolution time last quarter?" is a SQL question. Retrieval finds documents; it does not count rows. Give the agent a database tool instead.
  • Determinism is mandatory. Compliance checklists and financial calculations want code, not prose. Use the model to route or explain, never to compute.

A minimal rollout plan

  1. Write 20 real questions with verified answers. Build the retrieval harness first.
  2. Ingest the corpus with structure-aware chunking (380/50 as the documented start) and record the embedder version.
  3. Ship hybrid retrieval with re-ranking. Measure recall@k on the fixed set.
  4. Add faithfulness scoring. Gate it in CI next to recall.
  5. Add exact and semantic caching. Add citations to the UI. Add tenant scoping with a CI guard if you are multi-tenant.
  6. Deploy behind human review, read the failure cases weekly, and re-baseline the eval set quarterly.

RAG is unglamorous engineering: parsing, indexing, measuring, gating. The teams that treat it as such get systems users trust. The teams that treat it as "just embed the docs and chat" get demos that rot. If you want a second pair of eyes on a RAG design before you build it, get in touch; a short review often prevents a quarter of rework.

essays.title: How Long Does It Take to Build an AI Agent? An Honest Timeline
essays.excerpt: How long does it take to build an AI agent? A narrow automation lands in a week or two; a production agent with tools, guardrails and evals runs two to four weeks.
essays.body:
The short answer

The honest answer to how long it takes to build an AI agent is that it depends on the definition of done, not on the model. A narrow automation, one workflow with a clear trigger and a clear output, can land inside a week or two. A production agent with tool access, guardrails and an eval suite typically runs the full fixed-scope window of two to four weeks. A multi-tenant product with roles, permissions and admin surfaces runs longer than that, and Estate360-class scope is the honest shape of that situation.

For calibration, look at GAP Miner: it went from a 10-day manual research workflow to roughly 15 seconds of automated analysis. It got there because the scope was cut to one narrow job before any code was written, not because the model was magic. The case study lives at kunjshah.in/projects/gap-miner.

The same math shows up everywhere in agent delivery. A proof of concept that reads a single inbox and drafts replies is an afternoon of wiring plus real time on evals, data cleaning and review until it is trustworthy. The model was never the bottleneck; the workflow around it is. When someone quotes you a quarter for "an AI agent", they are usually quoting the data plumbing, the permission model and the review loop, not the inference call.

Anyone who quotes you a single number for "an AI agent" is selling, not estimating. The real drivers are the size of the workflow, the state of your data and how fast decisions get made on your side. Two engagements with identical model stacks can differ by weeks based on those three things alone.

The four steps, in order

Every fixed-scope engagement I run follows the same sequence, and each step exists to remove a specific failure mode. Skip a step and you do not save time; you defer the cost to a worse week.

  1. A 15-minute intro call. We look at the workflow, the data, the systems involved and the cost of getting it wrong. If the fit is bad, I say so on the call. No pitch deck, no obligation.
  2. Written scope with a fixed INR price before work starts. You get the scope in writing with a fixed price, so there is no invoice surprise and no moving target. Fixed-scope work starts at ₹25,000 and is typically delivered in two to four weeks. Payment is 40% upfront and 60% on delivery. If you prefer hourly, the rate is ₹1,500 per hour. If you need ongoing coverage after delivery, the retainer runs ₹30,000 to ₹75,000 per month.
  3. Build in your repository, on your cloud. From the first commit, the code lives in your repo and deploys to your cloud account. When the project ends, you own the code, the prompts, the eval suite and the deployment scripts. Nothing is held hostage on my machine, and your team can audit every decision because the history is yours.
  4. Handover with two revision rounds. The agent ships deployed, tested and logged, with a handoff document that explains what it does, what it refuses to do, and how to operate and debug it. Two rounds of revision are included, so the last mile is not a negotiation.

What makes it fast

Four things compress a build more than any technical choice. If you do these well, the two to four week window is realistic rather than optimistic.

  • A written definition of done. Not "the agent works", but the exact inputs, outputs, edge cases and quality bar that count as done. If we disagree on what done means, we find out in week one instead of week four.
  • A small labeled eval set up front. Twenty to fifty real examples with known-good answers. This turns "it seems to work" into a number, and it lets every change be measured instead of vibes-tested.
  • Read-only access to real data early. Agents fail on the data you forgot to mention. Read-only access in the first days exposes the missing columns, the encoding issues and the duplicate records before they become rework.
  • One decision-maker on your side. One person who can say yes, one who can say no, ideally the same person. Committees add weeks; a single owner removes them.

What stretches it

These are the six failure modes I see most often, in rough order of how much damage they do to a timeline.

Auth and permissions. Every permission system is bespoke. SSO, role hierarchies, least-privilege tokens, audit logs: these are engineering problems, not configuration problems. If the agent must act on behalf of different users with different rights, expect the auth layer to rival the agent layer in effort. Do not let it be improvised at the end.

Messy or missing data. The demo data is clean. Your production data is not. Duplicates, stale rows, free-text fields that quietly contain three comma-separated values, PDFs scanned at a slight angle. Data cleanup is unglamorous and it is usually where the hidden weeks live.

Third-party API instability and rate limits. When your agent depends on an external API, their outage is your outage and their rate limit is your rate limit. Retries, backoff, caching and graceful degradation all have to be designed, not bolted on. A flaky upstream can double the test matrix and eat the buffer you thought you had.

Compliance and review loops. Legal, security and privacy review add real time, and they should. If the agent touches personal data or customer communications, plan for review cycles and make sure the reviewers see the guardrails and the eval results, not just the polished demo.

An unclear definition of done. "Make the support agent better" is not a deliverable. Without explicit acceptance criteria, every demo is a fresh negotiation and the project never closes. This is the most common and the most expensive stretch factor.

Scope creep. One more tool, one more integration, one more "while you are in there". Each addition is individually reasonable and collectively fatal to a fixed timeline. Fixed scope exists to protect both of us from this, and the written change-request path is not bureaucracy; it is the mechanism that keeps the date honest.

Why not just buy a SaaS agent?

Fair question, and the honest answer cuts both ways.

Build when the workflow is yours. If the process, the data or the definition of quality is specific to your business, off-the-shelf tools will approximate it badly. Building is right when your data is sensitive and cannot leave your cloud, when the workflow crosses three systems no single vendor covers, and when the quality bar is yours to define. That is the situation fixed-scope builds are for, and it is why the code lands in your repository from day one.

Buy when the workflow is generic. If your need is drafting replies to common support tickets or summarizing meeting notes, a SaaS tool probably does it well enough and far cheaper than a custom build. Do not pay for bespoke engineering to avoid reading a pricing page. If the tool fits, buy it and spend the savings on the workflow it does not cover.

The middle ground is common: buy the commodity layer, build the differentiating one. The eval set is the tiebreaker. If you cannot articulate how you would measure the bought option, you are not ready to buy or build either; start with the evaluation, then decide. A vendor that refuses to be measured against your data is telling you something.

A useful rule of thumb from the field: if a SaaS tool covers most of your workflow out of the box and the remaining edge cases are politically important, buy the tool and build around it. If that remaining slice is where all the value lives, the tool is a distraction and a custom build is the honest answer.

How to keep yours on schedule

Schedule discipline is not about working faster. It is about removing the decisions that stall.

  • Fixed scope and fixed price, agreed in writing before the first commit.
  • Definition of done in writing, with acceptance criteria you can point at.
  • A weekly demo: thirty minutes, real data, real screen. Short feedback loops beat perfect plans.
  • One owner on your side with authority to accept delivery.
  • The eval set reviewed and signed off in week one, so every later change has a scoreboard.

If any of these are impossible on your side, a longer or phased engagement is not a failure; it is the correct estimate. The wrong estimate is the one that pretends the constraint does not exist and then rediscovers it in week three.

The practical next step

If you have a workflow in mind, bring it to a 15-minute call. I will tell you honestly whether it is a week, a month or a rewrite, and if it is out of scope for what I do, I will say that too. Fixed quote in writing, no surprises. Reach me at kunjshah.in/contact or kunjkshah05@gmail.com.

essays.title: YOLOv8 vs TensorRT: From Trained Model to Sub-100ms on Edge Hardware
essays.excerpt: YOLOv8 vs TensorRT is the wrong fight: model family and inference runtime compose. Inside the PyTorch to INT8 pipeline shipped on Jetson Orin for rail defect detection.
essays.body:
If you are searching "YOLOv8 vs TensorRT", the useful answer up front is that they are not competitors. YOLOv8 is a family of object-detection models you train. TensorRT is NVIDIA's inference runtime that executes a trained model fast on a specific GPU. The real question is not which one to pick; it is whether your trained model, exported and optimized through TensorRT, meets your latency, power and accuracy budget on the hardware you actually have.

This guide walks through the pipeline I shipped for railway defect detection on NVIDIA Jetson Orin, when TensorRT pays off, what INT8 quantization really costs, and the limits nobody puts on the box. Everything here comes from building the railway inspection system, not from benchmarks run on a datacenter GPU with a batch of 64.

What each piece actually is

YOLOv8 is the model family: convolutional detection networks with anchor-free heads, trained supervised on labeled images (faults, defects, anomalies). You get weights and an architecture. Out of the box on a desktop GPU it is fast; on edge hardware with a power envelope, "fast" is not automatically "inside budget".

TensorRT is a compiler and runtime. It takes an exported graph (commonly ONNX), fuses layers, selects kernels for the target GPU, and emits an engine: a serialized, hardware-specific plan that executes with minimal per-call overhead. Engines are the unit of deployment and the unit of lock-in.

ONNX is the interchange format between training and inference. You train in PyTorch, export to ONNX, and hand that to TensorRT. Keeping this boundary clean is what lets you retrain without redesigning the deployment.

The pipeline that shipped: training to sub-100ms on the track

The railway inspection system runs on a Jetson Orin mounted on inspection hardware, watching track footage for defects. The full chain:

  1. PyTorch training of the YOLOv8 detector on labeled track imagery.
  2. ONNX export of the trained graph for TensorRT ingestion.
  3. TensorRT engine build targeting the Orin's GPU, with layer fusion and kernel selection handled by the builder.
  4. INT8 quantization via quantization-aware training (QAT), so the model learns weights that survive 8-bit representation instead of being crushed after the fact.
  5. Hand-written CUDA kernels for the pre and post-processing stages where TensorRT cannot help you, because NMS and custom decode logic still need to be fast.
  6. GStreamer hardware decode to pull video frames in without burning CPU on software decoding.

Measured results on the deployed system: 98.7% accuracy, 4.2x faster than manual inspection, under 100ms per inference, and INT8 delivering roughly 2x the throughput of FP16. Those numbers are from a fixed railway-track context with controlled lighting and motion; treat them as a data point for that setting, not as a universal constant for your video.

Measuring correctly on device

Two measurement traps catch teams repeatedly. First, benchmarking on files instead of the live decode path: GStreamer hardware decode changes the frame timing and memory pools, so an engine that looks fast over pre-decoded frames can miss budget in situ. Second, averaging over best-case frames: defects are rare, so a loop over clean frames flatters latency and hides jitter. Profile the full loop (decode, pre-process, inference, post-process) on real footage, log the tail latencies, and validate accuracy and speed together. A faster engine that drops a defect class is not faster; it is worse.

When TensorRT pays off, and when it does not

TensorRT is worth the build pipeline when all of these hold:

  • The target GPU is fixed and known (a Jetson Orin on a train, not "whatever the cloud gives us").
  • You need sustained batch-1, real-time inference (continuous video, not overnight batch).
  • Latency or power is a hard constraint: sub-100ms budgets, fanless operation, battery or generator-limited deployments.
  • The model architecture is stable for weeks or months, so engine builds amortize.

It is the wrong choice when you retrain weekly (every retrain means re-export and re-validate), when you are CPU-only (TensorRT does not help; use ONNX Runtime or a quantized CPU path), or when you are still in exploration and do not yet know which model family you will ship. The build step also forces discipline: fixed input shapes, explicit precision decisions, and hardware-specific validation. If that discipline is absent, the engine becomes a liability rather than an asset.

FP16 vs INT8, and quantization-aware training

FP16 is the safe default: minimal accuracy loss, roughly half the memory bandwidth of FP32, and a straightforward engine build. INT8 roughly doubles throughput over FP16 on the Orin, at the cost of quantization error, which matters most on small objects, low-contrast textures and the long tail of rare defect classes.

Post-training quantization (PTQ) calibrates on sample data and rounds weights; it is fast to try and fine for tolerant workloads. QAT is the commitment: you simulate quantization during training so the network adapts its weights to 8-bit representation. QAT recovers most of the accuracy PTQ loses, and it is what made sub-100ms with 98.7% accuracy simultaneously possible in our case. The price is training infrastructure and curated calibration data that actually represents deployment conditions: the lighting, motion blur and camera angle you will see on the track, not the tidy images from a labeling tool.

The real enemies on track are not the model's FLOPs. They are motion blur from vibration and speed, and low-light or harsh-glare exposure. Histogram equalization on the input pipeline was the single most effective mitigation for low-light frames, restoring contrast the detector could lock onto. No amount of TensorRT tuning fixes a frame with no usable signal.

The decision checklist

Answer these honestly before committing to an engine pipeline:

  1. Is the target hardware fixed and NVIDIA? If no, stop; TensorRT does not apply.
  2. Is the latency budget under 100ms or power a hard cap? If no, ONNX Runtime on the same GPU is simpler and good enough for many workloads.
  3. Is the model stable, or is the team retraining weekly? If it churns, stay on ONNX Runtime/PyTorch until it settles.
  4. Do you have representative calibration and validation data from the deployment environment? If not, budget data collection first; INT8 without it is a coin flip.
  5. Is there a GStreamer or equivalent hardware decode path for your camera source? If decoding is the bottleneck, kernel-tuning the network yields nothing.

All five yes: TensorRT with QAT INT8. Some no: stay on ONNX Runtime or PyTorch, and revisit when the answers change.

Honest limitations of the TensorRT path

  • INT8 needs representative calibration data. Calibrating on desk imagery and deploying on railhead footage is how you ship a model that passes in the lab and misses in the field.
  • Engines are tied to one GPU architecture and TensorRT version. An Orin engine is not an A100 engine; a TensorRT upgrade can force rebuilds and revalidation. Plan for this in CI and in your release checklist.
  • Retraining means re-exporting. Every model refresh re-runs export, engine build, QAT validation and on-hardware profiling. If your refresh cycle is faster than your validation pipeline, you will ship unvalidated engines or stop refreshing.
  • The win is workload-specific. The roughly 2x INT8-over-FP16 throughput and under-100ms latency are facts about this system on this track context. Measure on your own footage before promising numbers to anyone.

What I would tell a team starting this tomorrow

Train a baseline in PyTorch, export to ONNX, and measure on the actual Orin before writing a single CUDA kernel. Most teams discover the bottleneck is decode or pre-processing, not the network. Add INT8-QAT only after FP16 is validated end to end, because debugging quantization and pipeline issues simultaneously is miserable. Invest in histogram equalization and motion-blur mitigation as input-stage infrastructure, and keep a small holdout of ugly real-world frames as the final gate. The engine is the easy part; the data is the product.

If you want an on-device vision system built, measured and handed over with its runbook, get in touch. I ship these systems fixed-scope, in your repo and your cloud.

essays.title: Edge Computer Vision in the Field: What 98.7% Accuracy Actually Required
essays.excerpt: Edge computer vision in the field: what 98.7% detection accuracy required on real railway track footage, INT8 TensorRT, GStreamer decode, Jetson Orin, under 100ms end to end.
essays.body:
The gap between a laptop demo and a rail corridor

Real railway track footage is not the benchmark reel. A camera mounted on an inspection vehicle sees a different world than a curated dataset: sun glare at dawn, long shadows across the rail head, sodium spill from trackside lights at night, motion blur at speed, ballast dust on the lens, the same perspective repeated for kilometres. Vibration adds its own special chaos, and every one of those conditions gets worse exactly when the inspection matters most.

This essay is about what it actually took to make detection work there, on the railway inspection deployment: real track footage, C++ and OpenCV, and a model that had to survive the corridor, not the conference room.

The reason this class of project is hard to buy is simple. Rail inspection is a measurement system wearing the costume of a vision product. If the number it produces cannot be trusted at speed in flat gray light, it is decoration; if it can, it changes how corridors get prioritized, how maintenance windows get scheduled and how many eyes you need on the track at all. That framing shapes every engineering decision below, from the quantization strategy to the threshold tuning.

The failure modes in the field are brutally specific. Ballast stones look like spalling. Shadows from overhead structures read as cracks. Motion blur smears the rail head into a gradient. Dust on the lens softens every edge the detector relies on. None of these appear in a clean dataset, and the first field test is always a humbling exercise in how much your training data flattered the model.

Why INT8, via quantization-aware training

The compute budget on an edge device is unforgiving, and the naive fix is to crush the model after training and pray. We did not do that. YOLOv8 was compiled to a custom TensorRT INT8 engine, and the INT8 quantization was produced with quantization-aware training, which means the model learned to be accurate at 8-bit precision instead of being forcibly truncated into it.

INT8 delivers roughly 2x the throughput of FP16 on this hardware, and with quantization-aware training the accuracy you keep is real, not a rounding error you discover in the field. That is the trade worth making when you need 98.7% detection accuracy inside a power and thermal envelope, because the alternative is a heavier model that misses its latency budget and never ships. If your vendor cannot tell you whether quantization was aware or merely applied, you have your answer about their process.

Post-hoc quantization, the "just convert it and hope" school, typically survives on benchmarks and dies on field footage. Quantization-aware training simulates the lower precision during training itself, so the weights settle into a representation that survives the rounding. The result is not a model that happens to fit INT8; it is a model that was trained to live there. On a rail corridor, where the input distribution swings with weather and speed, that margin is the difference between a system and a slide.

The decode problem

The model is never the whole system. Frames have to arrive, get decoded, get pre-processed, reach the network and leave as decisions, all inside a frame budget. We used GStreamer hardware decode so the GPU is not starved waiting on the CPU to unpack the stream, and the pipeline design matters as much as the model: a starving decoder means the most expensive component idles while frames queue up and latency quietly doubles.

The hot paths were hand-written CUDA kernels for the pre and post-processing work that frameworks refuse to fuse. C++ and OpenCV held the pipeline together. The result runs on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin and stays under 100ms end to end, which is the difference between a live inspection and a fancy recorder that tells you about the crack after the train passed it.

The shape of the pipeline is the lesson people skip. Decode on the hardware block, zero-copy the frame into device memory, pre-process there, infer, post-process there, emit. Any copy across the CPU-GPU boundary for a reason you cannot name is latency you are donating. GStreamer earns its place because the hardware decode path keeps the GPU fed at line rate, and without it the model starves no matter how fast the INT8 engine is.

Measuring honestly

The headline 98.7% detection accuracy is measured on held-out track footage, not on the clips the model was trained on. That distinction is the whole ballgame. Training-set accuracy is a measure of memory; held-out accuracy is a measure of usefulness, and the eval set deliberately includes motion blur cases, because blur is the condition that separates a railway inspection system from an aerial photography hobby.

The system runs 4.2x faster than manual inspection, which is the metric that actually changes operations, not just benchmarks. And when choosing operating points, false positives and false negatives are not symmetric costs. A false negative, a missed defect, is a safety exposure on a live rail network. A false positive costs an unnecessary human look. So the thresholds lean toward catching defects and letting humans clear the maybes, because on a rail network the asymmetry of consequences is the spec.

Held-out is doing real work in that sentence. The eval footage came from corridors the model never saw during training, with the same cameras, the same speeds and the same weather distribution, and the motion-blur cases were kept in the set on purpose rather than filtered out as inconvenient outliers. If your eval set is easier than your deployment environment, your accuracy number is a compliment, not a measurement.

What still gets it wrong

Three failure modes remain, and they should be stated plainly rather than buried in a datasheet. Extreme low-light still defeats the system: histogram equalization helps with motion blur and low-light conditions, but it does not create photons that were never captured, and an underexposed frame is an underexposed frame. Novel defect classes not present in the training data will be missed, because an INT8 engine cannot generalize to physics it was never shown. And camera misalignment, a mounting bracket slowly shifting under vibration, silently degrades everything downstream while every internal metric looks fine.

The mitigations are operational, not magical. Low-light gets flagged as low confidence and routed to a human rather than averaged into the accuracy number. Novel classes get added to the eval set the moment a confident misclassification is caught in review, because yesterday's blind spot is tomorrow's regression test. Misalignment gets caught by periodic calibration checks against known references, which is unglamorous and absolutely non-negotiable for a measurement system.

Anyone selling edge computer vision without a paragraph like this one is selling a screensaver, not an inspection system. The honest deliverable names its blind spots so the operator can compensate for them.

What to ask a vendor claiming edge CV

If you are evaluating an edge computer vision vendor, ask four questions before you watch the highlight reel:

  • Show me the eval harness. Held-out footage, motion blur included, with the failure distribution laid out. If they cannot produce it, the accuracy number is marketing.
  • Show me the hardware and the latency. Which device, what pipeline, what end-to-end number under load. "Runs real-time" without a budget is not a claim, it is a vibe.
  • Show me the failure modes. Extreme low-light, novel defects, misalignment. A vendor who cannot name them has not found them, which means you will.
  • Show me the maintenance plan. Who re-quantizes when the model changes, who maintains the eval set, who notices the camera drifting. Edge systems rot quietly; the eval harness is the smoke detector.

One more question that separates field systems from lab demos: ask what happens when the system is wrong. A serious vendor answers with a routing policy, confidence thresholds, a human review loop and a retraining path. A shaky vendor answers with "the model is 98.7% accurate", which is a true sentence that explains nothing about a run under a shaded overpass when every frame came out gray.

The full build notes, the pipeline and the numbers are on the case study at kunjshah.in/projects/railway-inspection. If you have a corridor, a yard or a fleet you want inspected, talk to me at kunjshah.in/contact. Bring footage, not slideware.

essays.title: Why 3 of 4 Agent Success Claims Fail Verification (and What Fixed It)
essays.excerpt: Why do agent success claims fail verification? In a published lab run, 3 of 4 were false; verify from application state, not the agent's self-report, then gate releases.
essays.body:
The uncomfortable observation

In a published lab run, three of four agent success claims were false. The agents said they had completed the task. The application state said otherwise. This is not an exotic edge case. It is the default failure mode of a system that grades its own homework.

The pattern is always the same. The agent narrates a plausible story of success: "I have updated the record", "the form has been submitted", "the ticket is resolved". Somewhere inside that story, the tool call failed, the locator matched the wrong element, the session expired, or the database write was rejected. The agent did not notice, or noticed and talked itself into a success narrative, and the summary it produced was fiction written in a confident register.

It helps to name the recurring failure classes, because they repeat across domains:

  • Silent tool failure. The call returned an error, the agent logged it as a warning, and the narrative moved on as if nothing happened.
  • Wrong-target success. The action succeeded, but against the wrong row, the wrong element or the wrong tenant. The system reports green while the world changed in the wrong place.
  • Unverified completion. The agent did the steps, never checked the outcome, and reported victory anyway because the plan said the steps were the work.

The summary is written by the component with the least reliable view of reality. The agent sees its own intended actions, not their consequences. That is the whole problem in one sentence, and it is why the demo always works and the audit never does.

Here is what a false success looks like from the outside. A support team deploys an agent to close tickets that match a resolution template. The dashboard shows a record close rate and a cheerful weekly summary.
