Then a customer calls about a refund that was promised but never issued, and the trail leads back to an agent that marked the ticket resolved because the draft reply was generated, not because the refund API returned success. Nobody lied on purpose. The system simply never checked.

Why LLM-as-judge does not save you here

The obvious rebuttal is to add a second model to grade the first. It helps for style, tone and completeness. It does not help for ground truth, because the judge has the same blind spot: it reads the transcript, and the transcript is exactly where the lie lives.

Ask a judge to evaluate "the refund was processed" from a conversation in which the refund API returned 409 Conflict, and the judge will produce a plausible verdict from the prose alone. It cannot see the missing ledger entry. It cannot see the DOM still showing "Refund pending". It has no privileged access to the application's records, so it defaults to the only signal it has: the fluency and specificity of the writing.

Worse, judges drift toward agreement. The agent's narrative is fluent and specific, and fluency reads as competence. A judge that disagrees with a confident, detailed account must muster its own confidence on weaker evidence, and it rarely does. If you want verification, you have to move the source of truth out of the context window and into the application's own records, where the claim can be checked instead of admired.

The fix: verify from the application's records

The Walkcast harness takes the position that the application is the referee. Instead of trusting the agent's self-report, it pins the failing step and captures before and after application state: the database rows, the DOM state and the API responses. If the agent claimed the invoice was marked paid but the row still reads pending, the claim is false, full stop. No adjudication by a second language model required.

The method is deliberately boring, which is why it works:

  1. Snapshot the relevant state before the action: rows, DOM nodes, response payloads.
  2. Let the agent act.
  3. Snapshot the same state after the action.
  4. Diff the two. The claim is verified only if the diff shows the intended change and nothing unintended rode along with it.

This is the same epistemology software has used for decades: state is what matters, not intention. Type systems, assertions, integration tests, monitoring. Agents do not get an exemption from verification because they are articulate. They get the same treatment as any other untrusted writer to your system, which is exactly what they are.

One detail in that design is load-bearing: pinning the failing step rather than checking only the final outcome. Coarse end-to-end checks tell you that something diverged somewhere. A pinned-step diff tells you that one step in the middle of the flow claimed a write and the database never saw it, which is the difference between a mystery and a Monday morning fix.

The full design and the numbers live at kunjshah.in/projects/walkcast.

Turning failures into permanent gates

Catching a false success once is useful. Making sure it can never ship silently again is the real prize. The same recorder turns a failed run into a classified, reproducible regression fixture: the failing step, the expected state, the actual state and a classification of what went wrong. Those fixtures run as a CI release gate, which means a new agent version must prove it fixed the bug and broke nothing else before it ships.

Two properties make this more than a test suite. First, fixtures are born from real failures, so they encode the ways your application actually breaks, not the ways a test author imagined in a planning meeting. Second, the gate is binary: the release either proves the fix or it does not. There is no "mostly working" badge on a release that fails the fixture set.

The live metrics on the case study: 75% false-success claims caught, 100% of injected faults reproduced and 129 test cases. That is what "tested" means when you build the harness from application state rather than from transcripts and hope.

What this means for teams buying agent work

If you are evaluating an agent vendor or a contractor, skip the demo video. Ask three questions instead:

  • Can I see the eval set, what is in it, and how were the examples chosen?
  • What is the release gate, and does it run in CI on every change?
  • When the agent fails, how do you reproduce the failure and prevent it permanently?

Teams that cannot answer these are demoing, not delivering. A demo shows the happy path with the lights on, the network healthy and the test account pre-seeded. An eval harness shows what happens when the locator is stale, the session expires, the API throttles and the agent is certain it finished the job.

A reasonable acceptance clause for any agent deliverable: no fixture, no fix. If a defect is found in acceptance testing, it becomes a fixture before it becomes a patch, so the fix is proven and the regression is gated forever. That single clause changes the incentive structure of the whole engagement, because every defect now makes the system permanently harder to break. It also protects you from the classic endgame where a vendor patches the symptom before the demo, the same failure resurfaces a month later, and nobody can prove the fix ever shipped.

Honest limits

State checks cover the happy path you recorded, and they cover it well. Novel failure modes, the ones nobody has imagined yet, still need human review. Fixtures also rot: when the application changes underneath them, the before and after snapshots no longer match reality, and a green gate becomes a false comfort. Gate maintenance is real work, and any team that tells you otherwise is selling something.

There is also a scope limit worth naming: state verification proves that the intended change happened. It does not prove the change was wise, compliant or reversible. An agent that deletes the right record for the wrong reason still passes the diff. Human review remains the control for intent, and intent is where the expensive mistakes live.

The correct posture is layered: state verification as the floor, human review for the unknown, and an honest admission that agents are probabilistic systems wearing the costume of determinism. None of this makes agents unusable. It makes them verifiable, which is the only version worth shipping.

essays.title: My OWASP Journey: What 60+ Merged PRs Taught Me About Shipping Secure Agents
essays.excerpt: My OWASP journey: what 60+ merged PRs across 24 external repositories taught me about shipping secure agents, security-regression CI and AGENTS.md as a control.
essays.body:
Why I started contributing to OWASP

Agent systems fail open. When an agent can read a repository, run tools and call APIs, the blast radius of a bad instruction or a poisoned dependency is not theoretical. The model will not pause to ask whether the action it is about to take is wise; it will take the action, narrate it confidently and move on. Security cannot be bolted on after the demo works, because by then the architecture has already decided what it trusts.

I started contributing to OWASP because the projects I was building needed the same rigor the OWASP community applies to web applications, applied to agent tooling. Web security matured by encoding known vulnerability classes into tests and pipelines. Agent security is earlier in that curve, and the people building the harnesses right now get to decide whether "the agent said it was fine" ever counts as evidence again.

The other honest reason: I wanted my work reviewed by people whose only incentive is the quality of the patch. Client work teaches you to ship. Open source teaches you to survive review.

Consider what happens inside a repository where an agent can run tools. A coding agent is asked to fix a failing test. It finds the test, decides the test is wrong, edits it, and reports the suite green. Nobody attacked anything. The agent simply optimized for the proxy metric, which is the suite passing, not the bug being gone. Multiply that by every repo your agents touch and you have the everyday version of the problem, no adversary required.

What merged work actually looks like

Sixty plus merged PRs across 24 external repositories, including work merged in the OWASP agent-security harness and Microsoft's AI-Engineering-Coach. The shape of that work is consistent, and it is deliberately unglamorous:

  • Small, reviewable diffs. One concern per PR. A reviewer who can hold the whole change in their head is a reviewer who actually reviews.
  • A stated threat model. What is being protected, from whom, and via which path. If the PR cannot name the threat, it is not a security PR; it is a refactor wearing a security badge.
  • Tests that encode the vulnerability class. Not "it works now", but "this class of failure can never silently pass again".
  • CI that fails on regression. A fix without a gate is a fix with an expiry date.

Merged work spans CI, security and agent tooling, which matters more than it sounds: agent systems sit at the intersection of build pipelines, application security and tool invocation, so the work that actually ships is the work that respects all three at once. Even the efficiency patches count here. My contribution to Ollama, issue #15639 on token calculation efficiency, cut wasted inference, because paying for tokens nobody reads is the same failure mode as trusting output nobody checks: resources spent without verification.

The mechanics of getting merged are worth naming, because they are the same mechanics as shipping secure agents. I read the project's contribution guide and issue tracker first, claim something small and well-scoped, and write the PR the way a reviewer would want to review it: minimal diff, tests that encode the problem, a description that states the threat model and the rollback story. Then I watch what reviewers ask for, and the pattern repeats until the review becomes boring. Boring review is the goal state of secure software.

The security-regression CI pattern

The pattern is simple to state and fiddly to do. Take a vulnerability class you have seen once. Encode it as a test: an input, a context, an expected-safe outcome. Wire that test into CI so the pipeline fails when the class reappears. From that moment, the vulnerability is not "fixed"; it is "prevented, forever, with evidence".

This is the same pattern I use in client work. When an agent discloses a secret, calls a forbidden tool or accepts an injected instruction, that incident becomes a fixture, the fixture becomes a CI gate, and the gate becomes part of the release checklist. I have built this muscle in public repositories where strangers could reject my work, which is the best possible training for building it in codebases where the stakes are real.

A security-regression workflow is not a one-off audit you commission and frame. It is a compounding asset: each fixed class becomes permanent immune memory for the codebase, and the pipeline enforces it without anyone having to remember.

AGENTS.md as a security control

One piece of that work is AGENTS.md documentation written for coding agents, so agents working in the repo follow the security rules. This sounds like documentation. It is not. It is an access control written in prose.

Agents are contributors now. They read the repository, run the tools, open the pull requests and respond to review comments. If your security guidance lives only in a wiki that humans forget to read, then your agent population is operating without guardrails, and it will faithfully follow the fastest path to "done". AGENTS.md moves the rules into the one place every agent actually opens: the root of the repository, before it touches anything.

Good agent instructions read like good onboarding for a new hire with root access: what must never happen, what must always happen, what to do when unsure, and where the escape hatch is. The difference is that the new hire asks questions and the agent improvises, so the written rules carry more weight, not less. A rule that is never written is a rule that does not exist, and the agent will fill the silence with its own judgment.

The practical effect in a repo with agents as contributors: reviewers stop re-litigating the same security basics on every PR, because the basics are enforced by the file the agent reads first. The PR conversation moves from "please do not do X" to "X is already impossible here, check the CI output".

What this means when hiring me

Security review is built into the delivery, not a paid add-on. Every engagement ships with threat-modeled PRs, CI regressions for the classes we touch and an honest limitations section that names what the system does not protect against. That section is not an admission of weakness; it is the difference between a system you can operate and a system you can only demo.

The open-source record is also the audit trail. Sixty plus merged PRs across 24 repositories, 4 hackathon finals and 17+ shipped systems means the review habit is not a claim on a website; it is a public, checkable history, including the Ollama efficiency work described above. Efficiency and security are the same discipline seen from different angles: waste nothing, trust nothing, verify everything.

If you are buying agent work, the security story should not be a paragraph in a proposal. It should be visible in the repository: the regression fixtures, the CI gate, the AGENTS.md, the limitations section. Ask to see them. If a vendor cannot produce them, you know exactly what you are buying.

Concretely, for a fixed-scope engagement, that means the security surface is part of the estimate rather than a line item negotiated later: the threat model is written before the first prompt is drafted, the regression fixtures are part of the test plan, and the handoff document includes an honest limitations section and an operating runbook. The two to four week window is not compressed by skipping security; it is compressed because the security work is front-loaded, small and verifiable, the same way it merged in public repositories.

The honest note

Open source taught me that reviewers merge what they can verify, the same standard I apply to agent output. Your patch is not merged because you believe in it, because the author is charming, or because the deadline is Friday. It is merged because a stranger can check it, run it and trust the result. That is the correct standard for agent systems too.

It also taught me the limit of my own taste. There is no authority in review except evidence, and the reviewer does not care how elegant your solution felt at 2 AM. The same applies when an agent reports success: the report is a claim, the diff is the evidence, and the gate is the judge. Everything in this essay reduces to that one rule, applied patiently, in public and in private, until it becomes instinct.

essays.title: Semantic vs Exact Caching for LLM APIs: What Actually Pays Off
essays.excerpt: Semantic vs exact caching for LLM APIs: what actually pays off, why semantic sits on top of exact, and when to skip caching entirely.
essays.body:
LLM caching is not normal caching, and teams that treat it as "Redis with extra steps" either cache nothing (paying full price forever) or cache the wrong thing (serving a confidently wrong answer to a different user). The short version up front: exact caching pays for itself immediately, semantic caching only makes sense layered on top of exact caching, and if you cannot measure your wrong-hit rate, the semantic layer is on probation. This essay is the playbook I use, drawn from two systems I have shipped: OnRamp, where every model call goes through a free-tier-first router with exact and semantic Redis caches behind it, and Estate360, a multi-tenant real estate CRM where an exact cache carries about a one hour TTL, semantic hits live for 24 hours, and semantic serving requires a 0.85 similarity threshold.

Projects: OnRamp and Estate360.

Why LLM caching is different

Three properties make LLM workloads unusually cacheable. Outputs are deterministic-ish (especially at temperature zero or near it). Real traffic is not a smooth distribution; it is a spike of near-identical requests. And the requests that repeat are exactly the expensive ones: support answers, document Q and A, onboarding checklists, the same questions rephrased by every new user. If your traffic looks like "what does this error mean", "how do I connect X", or "summarize this policy", the repeat rate is high enough that caching moves the bill, not just the dashboard.

What breaks the analogy with HTTP caching is correctness. Serving a stale image is mildly annoying; serving a stale or near-miss LLM answer can be actively wrong, confidently delivered. That is why the whole design is shaped around one question: how wrong can a hit be, and how would we know?

Exact caching: the free money

Exact caching is trivially safe and almost always worth doing first. Hash the normalized prompt plus the model plus the temperature, and serve the stored completion on a hash match. Normalization means trimming whitespace, collapsing case where your domain allows it, and pinning everything else. When the hash matches, the request is the same request, and the answer is the answer the model would (probably) give again.

  • Safety: zero risk of wrong-answer injection. A hit is a bitwise repeat of a request already served.
  • Hit rate: enormous on FAQ-shaped traffic and document Q and A; smaller on long, personalized generations.
  • TTL by volatility: Estate360 keeps exact matches around for about an hour. Volatile content (prices, inventory, statuses) should expire fast; stable content (policy text, architecture docs) can live longer.
  • Invalidation is key-scoped: change the prompt template and the hashes change; old entries rot naturally instead of poisoning new traffic.

Normalization deserves real care, because it decides what "the same request" means. Trim and collapse whitespace, unify quote and dash characters, canonicalize casing for case-insensitive domains, strip volatile metadata (timestamps, session ids, request ids) that would otherwise guarantee a miss. Keep the normalization versioned alongside the template version: change the normalizer and every old key becomes unreachable. The failure mode of sloppy normalization is silent 0% hit rate with all the machinery still running, which is the most expensive way to cache nothing.

Ship exact caching behind a flag, log every hit and miss, and let it run. It is the highest certainty dollar in the whole cost-reduction stack.

Semantic caching: real gains, real failure mode

Semantic caching serves the nearest prior answer to a rephrased request. Both systems I run do this with hashed n-gram cosine similarity over prompts rather than full embeddings; the mechanism is cheap, local and good enough to catch "how do I reset my password" versus "password reset steps". Semantic hits in Estate360 are kept for 24 hours and require a 0.85 similarity threshold. That number is not decoration. At 0.7 you serve answers to questions nobody asked; at 0.85 you mostly serve the same question asked politely and impolitely.

PropertyExact cacheSemantic cache
Match ruleHash of normalized prompt + model + temperatureNearest neighbor above 0.85 cosine similarity over hashed n-grams
Typical TTL (Estate360)About 1 hour24 hours
Failure modePractically none; misses are just missesNear-miss answer served confidently to a materially different question
Best forFAQ-shaped traffic, repeated templatesRephrasings of the same underlying question

The one rule I will not bend: semantic caching only makes sense on top of exact caching, never instead of it. Exact is your correctness floor; semantic is an optimization you add after the floor exists and you can measure above it.

Invalidation: where caches go to lie

A cache without an invalidation story is a wrong-answer generator with good uptime. My rules:

  1. Prompt template changes bust the cache. Version your templates and fold the version into the key. The day you tweak the system prompt, every cached answer under the old version is suspect.
  2. TTLs follow content volatility, not vibes. Onboarding checklist: long. Support macro about a pricing page that changes quarterly: short. Estate360 splits 1h exact and 24h semantic as a sane default, not a law.
  3. Never cache tool side effects. Caching the model's text is fine; caching the act of "book the site visit" or "send the reminder" is not a cache, it is a skipped action with plausible text attached.
  4. Never share personal data across users or tenants. Cache keys must include the tenant scope where the prompt can carry tenant data. OnRamp's onboarding answers can be shared across repos; Estate360's answers about a customer's units cannot be shared across workspaces, ever.
  5. Model and temperature are part of the key. Swap the model without busting keys and you are serving the old model's habits under the new model's name.

Rollout order, so you do not cache yourself into a corner

Ship this in the order that keeps blast radius small. First, exact caching behind a feature flag, hit and miss logged, for one workflow at a time; support answers or document Q and A are ideal. Second, watch the hit rate and the cost curve for a couple of weeks; if exact caching is not moving the needle on your traffic mix, semantic will not save you. Third, add the semantic layer behind the same flag, with the 0.85 threshold and spot checks running from day one. Fourth, widen coverage tenant by tenant or workflow by workflow, and keep the off switch one flag away. Teams that flip semantic caching on globally on day one are the teams that quietly serve wrong answers and never find out.

Measuring: hit rate is a vanity metric until you add wrong-hit rate

Both systems ship cache hits as first-class telemetry, and so should yours. Three numbers, in order of importance:

  • Wrong-hit rate: the percentage of semantic hits that were near-misses, estimated by spot-checking a sample of served hits against what the model would have produced fresh. If you cannot measure this, semantic caching is on probation, full stop.
  • Cost saved: tokens avoided, priced per provider, trended weekly. This is the number your finance person cares about and your arguments to keep the cache alive.
  • Hit rate: useful for capacity planning and for spotting traffic-mix shifts. A sudden drop means the product changed under the cache, not that the cache got worse.

Exact cache hits need no wrong-hit rate; they are repeats. Semantic hits need continuous spot checks, forever, because the input distribution drifts and 0.85 is a threshold, not a guarantee.

In practice I run the wrong-hit audit like a tax audit: a fixed sample of served semantic hits, re-answered fresh by the model, with a human or a strict grader marking each pair as same-answer, close-enough or wrong. The close-enough bucket is the dangerous one, because it feels fine in aggregate and poisons trust one user at a time. Track the wrong share weekly; if it creeps, raise the threshold or shrink the TTL before you debug anything else.

When to skip caching entirely

  • Low traffic. Below some modest volume, the engineering and observability cost exceeds the tokens saved.
  • Highly personalized prompts. If every prompt embeds the user's unique context, hit rates collapse and you pay cache-lookup overhead for nothing.
  • Compliance-sensitive output. If a stale or near-miss answer creates regulatory exposure, the correct cache TTL is zero.
  • No telemetry. If you cannot see hits, misses and wrong-hits, you are flying blind with a correctness risk attached.

The short version

Hash everything first, serve repeats for free, then add semantic serving behind a high threshold with spot checks and honest telemetry. Cache text, never actions; scope keys by tenant; bust on template changes. If your LLM bill is dominated by repeated questions, this is the cheapest real engineering you can do. If your traffic is all bespoke, skip it and spend the effort on prompt quality instead.

I build caching layers and cost-control stacks like this for production LLM products. Fixed scope from ₹25,000, fixed quote in writing, free 15-minute intro call: https://kunjshah.in/contact.

essays.title: The Multi-Provider Fallback Playbook for LLM Outages
essays.excerpt: The multi-provider fallback playbook for LLM outages: chain design, timeout budgets, a zero-key heuristic floor, and when not to bother.
essays.body:
Every LLM provider has outages, and every provider has rate limits. If your product calls exactly one, you have inherited their risk posture as your own. When Groq rate-limits at 2am or a free endpoint silently starts queuing, your users do not see "provider degraded"; they see your product failing. The multi-provider fallback playbook is how you build a product that degrades to a weaker answer instead of an error page, and it is the architecture behind two systems I ship: ArchMind, which runs a six-provider fallback chain ending in an 18-rule heuristic engine that needs zero API keys, with a keep-warm GitHub Actions workflow to keep the free endpoints alive, and ResumeMasterAI, which sits behind the routing gateway I wrote about earlier. This essay is the pattern, including the unglamorous parts.

Projects: ArchMind AI and ResumeMasterAI.

The premise

Single-vendor AI products are single points of failure wearing a nice UI. Provider risk is not hypothetical: rate limits, regional incidents, deprecated models, pricing changes, silent latency degradation. Any one of these can take a feature from "works" to "errors out" without your deploy logs showing a thing, because you changed nothing; the world did.

The design goal is not "99.999% uptime" (I will not quote a number I cannot defend). The goal is that when a provider fails, the user gets a worse answer, not an error. Every failure path ends in a weaker answer, never an error page.

The economics help too. OnRamp opens with free tiers and a full nine-step autopilot run ends up cheaper than one paid call, which means the fallback chain and the cost model are the same mechanism. Building the chain is not resilience theatre bolted onto an expensive product; it is the cheapest way to keep a multi-provider product alive while the invoice stays near zero. The lesson from OnRamp is blunt: model routing is a cost-control problem before a capability problem, and the same logic applies to ordering failover tiers.

The chain design

ArchMind runs: Groq, then NVIDIA, then OpenRouter, then Gemini, then Ollama, then HuggingFace, then an 18-rule heuristic engine. Estate360 runs a tighter pool: Groq, Gemini, Mistral, NVIDIA. OnRamp routes free-tier-first: OpenRouter, Gemini, Groq and NVIDIA up front, with DeepSeek, Qwen, Zhipu, Moonshot, Mistral, OpenAI, Anthropic, HuggingFace and Ollama behind.

The order is not arbitrary. Design the chain by three axes, in this order:

  1. Cost. Free and cheap tiers first, paid tiers behind. This is why ArchMind and OnRamp lead with free tiers, and why OnRamp's whole economics hold: a full autopilot run ends up cheaper than one paid call.
  2. Latency. Fast providers early for interactive paths; slow but capable providers later for batch.
  3. Capability. The deepest reasoning model is not first in the chain; it is reserved for the queries that need it, which is the routing problem, not the fallback problem.

Mechanics that matter:

  • Per-query-type chains. OnRamp routes per query type rather than with one global chain; a classification call and a synthesis call do not deserve the same fallback order.
  • Health checks and circuit breakers. If a provider starts failing or latency-spiking, trip the breaker and skip it for a cooldown window instead of paying the timeout on every request.
  • Timeout budgets, not infinite patience. Each hop gets a budget; when it expires, fail over, do not retry forever.
  • Retry vs failover, decided in advance. Retry the same provider only for transient, idempotent failures (rate limit with a short reset, blip). Anything else, or repeated failure, fails over down the chain.
  • Log the decision. Every failover is logged with the reason. Without that log you cannot tune the chain or detect a provider slowly dying.
  • Health means signals, not pings. Watch error rate and latency on real traffic, not just whether the endpoint answers a synthetic hello. A provider can respond 200 and still be useless because every response is a queue timeout or a degraded model.
StageRole in chainWhen it serves
Groq / NVIDIA / OpenRouter / GeminiFree-tier first lineDefault traffic; fast, cheap, occasionally rate-limited
Ollama / HuggingFace / MistralSecondary free capacityWhen the front line trips or queues
DeepSeek / Qwen / Zhipu / Moonshot / OpenAI / AnthropicPaid and frontier tiersHard reasoning or when free tiers are exhausted
18-rule heuristic engine (ArchMind)Zero-key floorEvery provider unavailable; deterministic scored baseline

The floor: degraded but useful beats a 500

The single most important decision in ArchMind was the last link: not another provider, but a deterministic, 18-rule heuristic engine that requires zero API keys. When every provider in the chain is down, the product does not error out; it returns a scored, rule-based baseline. The lesson generalizes: every chain should terminate in something that cannot fail, even if that something is deliberately shallow. "Service degraded, here is the deterministic answer" beats a 500, beats a spinner that never resolves, and beats a blank page every single time.

Design your floor around what your product fundamentally does. For ArchMind it is rule-based architecture scoring. For a support bot it might be canned answers to the twenty most common intents. For a resume tool it might be deterministic checks (quantified impact present or absent, tense consistency). The floor will not impress anyone, and it is the reason nobody gets blocked.

Free-tier-first routing

Free-tier-first is routing applied to your fallback chain, and it inherits the same lesson I learned building ResumeMasterAI: model routing is a cost-control problem before a capability problem. Route by expected task difficulty; the easy 80% of queries never touch a paid model. Log which tier served each query; never silently swap models mid-session without logging. Silent swaps destroy your ability to answer the question "why did quality drop on Tuesday".

One warning: free tiers trade latency and rate limits for cost. That is the correct trade for batch and forgiving-UX paths, and the wrong trade for latency-critical interactive flows. Put the SLO, not the price tag, in charge of the interactive path.

The unsexy parts (where fallback chains actually live or die)

  • Keep-warm pings. ArchMind runs a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow to keep the free endpoints alive. Free tiers that sleep or throttle on idle will fail you exactly when traffic arrives.
  • Alerting on fallback rate. A rising fallback rate is your early warning that a provider is degrading. If nobody gets paged on it, the chain is decorative.
  • Budget caps per provider. A retry storm against a paid provider is a billing incident. Caps and alerts, always.
  • Kill switches. You need a way to disable a provider without a deploy, because the failure mode you are routing around is often an account or key problem, not code.
  • Test the failover like backups. Pull the plug on purpose, in staging, and watch what happens. ArchMind exercises the fallback chain in CI precisely because it is the part most likely to break. An untested fallback chain is a hypothesis, not a control.
  • Postmortem the failovers. When the chain fires in production, write down which link failed, how long detection took, and whether the floor served. Those notes are how the chain earns its keep; without them you are just hoping the next outage lands on a well-tested path.
  • Drill the cold case, not just the warm one. Most drills test the first failover hop. Also test the total collapse: every provider down, only the heuristic engine left, and confirm the product still answers with its deterministic baseline instead of an error page.

When not to build this

Honest scoping, because resilience machinery has a real cost:

  • Internal tools used by five people who can tolerate a retry: skip the chain, keep the provider interface abstraction.
  • A single provider with an SLA you actually trust (and budget for): the SLA is your fallback plan; know its terms.
  • MVPs where speed beats resilience: ship the happy path, abstract the provider interface anyway, and add the chain when the first provider wobble costs you a customer.

The abstraction is non-negotiable even when the chain is not: a thin provider interface costs days, and it converts "we are down until the vendor recovers" into a config change later.

The takeaway

Order the chain by cost, latency and capability. Give it a zero-key floor. Log every decision. Alert on fallback rate. Pull the plug monthly. And accept the trade honestly: you are buying resilience with complexity, and the only unforgivable version of this work is the one nobody has ever tested.

If you want a multi-provider LLM architecture that fails soft instead of hard, that is my work. Fixed scope from ₹25,000, fixed quote in writing, free 15-minute intro call: https://kunjshah.in/contact.

essays.title: Test-Enforced Tenant Isolation: Why Your Multi-Tenant SaaS Needs a CI Guard
essays.excerpt: Test-enforced tenant isolation: how a CI guard test fails the build when any query path in a multi-tenant SaaS lacks a workspaceId filter.
essays.body:
Multi-tenant SaaS on a shared Postgres schema is the default because it is cheap, simple and fast to ship: one database, one connection pool, one migration path, every customer's rows in the same tables with a workspaceId column telling you who owns what. It is also the architecture where one forgotten WHERE clause hands customer A the data of customer B. I learned this pattern the honest way while building Estate360, a multi-tenant real estate CRM for builders and brokerages, on a shared schema with every query scoped by workspaceId, and where the enforcement is not a code review checklist but a test that fails the build. This essay is the whole pattern, including the part nobody likes talking about: the RLS policies I wrote that do nothing.

The project: Estate360, built on Next.js 16, Prisma 7 and Supabase Postgres, with a Groq, Gemini, Mistral and NVIDIA fallback pool behind the AI surfaces.

Why shared-schema multi-tenancy is the default, and the danger

The alternatives are well known: a database per tenant, a schema per tenant, or a shared schema with a discriminator column. Database per tenant is operationally heavy at small scale; schema per tenant multiplies migration pain; shared schema with workspaceId is the pragmatic default. Pragmatic does not mean safe. Shared schema means the database will happily return any row to anyone who asks for it. The database does not know your tenancy model; only your queries do.

So the entire isolation story collapses to one question: can any code path reach tenant data without a workspaceId predicate? Everything else, the tests, the reviews, the policies, exists to answer that question continuously and automatically, not once at design time.

Belt and suspenders: app-layer scoping plus a CI guard

My defense is two layers that fail independently.

Layer one: app-layer scoping everywhere. Every query that touches a tenant-owned table includes the workspaceId predicate. Not most queries. Every one, including the boring ones in admin scripts and report generators, because attackers and bugs both specialize in the boring paths.

Layer two: a CI guard that treats an unscoped query as a build failure. Estate360 runs three tenant-scope test gates. The centerpiece is a static guard that scans every tenant-model call site in app/, lib/ and modules/ and fails the build if one lacks a workspaceId predicate. Exceptions are allowed, but they must be registered alongside a checkable reason, which means an exception is a visible, reviewed artifact, not a silent bypass. Two more tests assert that every tenant read path has a recorded broker-visibility decision, and that the broker predicate actually reaches Prisma rather than dying somewhere in the call chain. Vitest covers the units, Playwright covers the end-to-end flows.

The philosophy: scoping is necessary, but a human remembering to scope is not a control. A control is a machine that says no.

LayerWhat it doesWhat it misses
App-layer workspaceId scopingFilters every tenant query at the call siteDepends on every developer, every time, forever
CI guard testFails the build on any unscoped tenant-model call siteOnly sees call sites matching its scan rules; needs the two companion gates for visibility and predicate propagation
Postgres RLSDatabase-side policies as a backstopInert until the app connects as a role that does not own the tables and does not carry BYPASSRLS

The uncomfortable truth about RLS

Row Level Security is the answer everyone reaches for, and it is a good answer with one brutal precondition. Estate360 has RLS enabled and 31 policies written. They stay inert. The application connects as a role that owns every table and carries BYPASSRLS, so Postgres skips the policies entirely, whether or not they exist and whether or not they are correct.

Enabled is not enforced. If your app role owns the tables, or connects with BYPASSRLS, RLS is decoration: it documents intent, it audits well in a screenshot, and it stops exactly nothing. The real control lives in role separation. The app needs a dedicated role that does not own the tables and does not bypass RLS, plus a separate migration role that does own them. Estate360 has a switch for this, but it is gated by a script that refuses to proceed until its checks pass, because an untested role flip on a production tenant table is how you take the CRM down on a Tuesday.

Until that switch flips, query scoping is the only deployed isolation layer, and pretending otherwise is how breaches happen. I would rather state that plainly than gesture at 31 policies.

The CI guard pattern

If you take one thing from this essay, take the pattern, not the Postgres specifics. It generalizes.

  1. Enumerate the tenant-model call sites. Decide what counts as a tenant-model call (in my case, Prisma client calls against tenant-owned models) and scan the directories that can contain them: app/, lib/, modules/.
  2. Assert the predicate. Every scanned call site must contain a workspaceId filter, or a registered exception with a checkable reason. Unregistered equals fail.
  3. Add companion gates for the semantics the static scan cannot see. Ours verify two things: that every tenant read path records a broker-visibility decision, and that the broker predicate actually reaches Prisma. Static analysis checks shape; these check behavior.
  4. Fail the build on violation. Not a warning, not a lint with a quiet exit code. The PR does not merge.
  5. Add the guard before the first tenant, not after the incident. Retrofitting means deciding under pressure which unscoped paths are bugs and which are "load-bearing". Do it calmly, in an empty system, where the answer is always "fix it".

Testing that it actually works

One subtlety worth naming: Estate360 has a second isolation boundary inside each tenant. Brokers see a subset of the workspace, not all of it. Tenant A versus workspaceId scoping is the outer wall; broker visibility is an inner partition, and it is just as easy to get wrong. That is why two of the three gates exist: one asserts every tenant read path records a broker-visibility decision, and the other asserts that predicate actually reaches Prisma instead of being dropped somewhere in the call chain. If you only test the outer wall, you have secured the building and left the interior doors unlocked.

A guard you never see fail is a guard you do not understand. My test setup uses two test tenants seeded with different data, then asserts invisibility in both directions: tenant A cannot read tenant B's rows on any tenant read path, and tenant B cannot read tenant A's. Broker-scoped queries get the same treatment, because brokers see a subset within a tenant, which is a second isolation boundary that is just as easy to get wrong.

These tests run on every PR. The friction is the point. If a developer adds a new tenant read path without thinking about who is allowed to see it, the suite says no before review does. Review is for judgment; machines are for invariants.

Three tenant-scope gates in total: the static call-site scan, the visibility-decision check, and the predicate-propagation check. Each covers what the others cannot. No single test proves isolation; the triangle does.

Honest limitations

Application-layer filters are necessary but not sufficient, and this essay would be dishonest if it stopped at the CI guard. What still matters:

  • Audit logs. When something does leak, or almost leaks, you need to know which workspaceId, which path, which user. Isolation without auditability is blind.
  • Least-privilege DB roles. Even outside RLS, the app role should not hold DDL rights it never uses. Ownership and bypass flags are the whole ballgame for RLS, and they are also good hygiene on their own.
  • Backups and exports. A nightly dump is one giant unscoped read. Exports for a single tenant must carry the same workspaceId discipline as the app; a CSV download that ignores tenancy is a data leak with a friendly UI.
  • Tests prove the paths you scan. The guard knows about call sites matching its rules. New modules, new models, new raw SQL: each needs to be folded into the scan or the coverage quietly expires.

None of this is exotic. It is the same lesson every time: pick a small set of invariants, encode them in machines that say no, and be honest in your docs about which layers are deployed and which are written but inert.

I build and harden multi-tenant systems like this for real estate and other B2B workflows. Fixed scope from ₹25,000, fixed quote in writing, free 15-minute intro call. If you are shipping a shared-schema SaaS, the cheapest week of your life is the week the guard goes in, before the first tenant signs. Talk to me.

essays.title: Model Routing: How I Cut LLM API Spend 65% Without Hurting Quality
essays.excerpt: Model routing: how I cut LLM API spend 65% in production without hurting quality, with 3x match precision and under 200ms added latency per request.
essays.body:
Every AI product I have shipped eventually hits the same invoice problem: the bill grows because every single request pays flagship prices, including the thousands of requests that never needed a frontier model. ResumeMasterAI, my career platform for scoring and tailoring resumes against job descriptions, hit that wall hard. The fix was not a cheaper model and it was not a bigger discount from a provider. The fix was a routing gateway in front of the models, and it cut my API spend by 65% while actually improving output quality. Here is how it works, what I measured, and where it breaks.

The project is public: ResumeMasterAI is built on Python, LangGraph, an AI Gateway layer and ChromaDB, with the source at github.com/KunjShah01/job-snipper. What follows is the architecture, not a sales pitch.

The invoice problem

The naive architecture for an LLM feature is one model behind one endpoint. Every request, from "rewrite this bullet point" to "weigh four constraints across a career arc and propose a positioning strategy", goes to the same large model. It works, demos well, and then the first real invoice arrives.

The uncomfortable part is not the total. It is the distribution. A large fraction of the traffic in a production agent is shallow: short rewrites, extractions, formatting, classification, confirmation steps. These are tasks where a small, cheap model is not a compromise; it is the correct instrument. Paying flagship prices for them is pure waste, and it scales linearly with adoption.

There is a second-order problem too. A single hard-coded model couples your product to one provider's pricing, availability and rate limits. The invoice problem and the resilience problem have the same root cause: you have not told the system which requests are actually hard.

The insight: model size should match task complexity

The models are not the bottleneck. The allocation is. Task complexity varies enormously across requests, and model capability varies enormously across tiers, so the obvious move is to match them. Most of the time, the honest answer to "which model should handle this" is: the smallest one that clears the quality bar for this specific task, not the biggest one on the roadmap slide.

What changed in my head, building this, is that routing is a systems problem, not a model problem. You need a classifier, a routing policy, a checkpoint trail, an eval suite and a human review loop. Miss any one of those and the savings are imaginary or the quality quietly rots.

Request profileRouteWhy
Short rewrite, extract, classify, formatSmall, cheap modelShallow task; big model adds cost, not correctness
Retrieval-heavy answer from known docsSmall model plus retrievalThe work is in the context, not the reasoning
Multi-constraint reasoning, ambiguous briefLarge modelGenuine hard reasoning; this is what you pay the flagship for
Strict output structure, high stakesLarge model plus validationStructure violations are cheap to detect, expensive to miss

The implementation: classifier, route, checkpoint, spot-check

The gateway sits between the product logic and the providers. Every request passes through four stages.

1. The classifier reads the request, not the vibes

The complexity classifier looks at concrete, checkable signals: input length, task type, whether the request actually needs retrieval, and what output structure is required. No embeddings mysticism, no free-form judgment calls. A five-token "make this punchier" request and a paste of a full career history with three constraints never get scored the same way, because the inputs differ in ways that matter.

2. The router applies the policy

Easy, well-structured tasks go to small, cheap models. Hard reasoning, ambiguous briefs and strict structure requirements go to large models. The policy is explicit in code, versioned, and reviewable. When the policy is wrong, you fix the policy, not the prompt salad.

3. Checkpointing plus human-in-the-loop review

LangGraph gives me checkpoints at graph boundaries, so any run can be inspected, replayed or paused for human review. High-stakes outputs (a full tailored resume, say) can be gated on a review step instead of shipped blind. This is not bureaucracy; it is how you keep a cheap routing decision from becoming an expensive customer-facing mistake.

4. Spot-checks close the loop

Every routing decision is logged: the classifier's read of the request, the model chosen, the latency, the cost, and the downstream quality signal where one exists. A sample of those logs gets human review. That is the raw material for tuning the classifier and for catching quiet quality drift.

Measuring it honestly

Anyone can claim savings. The measurement discipline is the product. Three numbers came out of the routing gateway work: API cost dropped 65%, match precision improved 3x, and the routing layer adds under 200ms per request.

A few things about how to read those numbers without bullshit. Cost is measured per successful task, not per request. If the cheap model produces garbage and the user retries, you paid twice and saved nothing; the metric that matters is cost per task that actually completes and is accepted. Quality was held by an eval suite plus human review, not by faith in the classifier. The quality floor is the constraint; cost is the variable you optimize under it.

And the 3x precision figure deserves the honest footnote: it came from the routing gateway and its bounded agent steps, not from a magic model. Small models handle the shallow work they are actually good at, large models get reserved for genuine reasoning, and the step count is bounded so the agent cannot wander. Better allocation, better outputs. Anyone selling you a "smarter model" for that gain is hiding the real mechanism.

The catch

Routing is a cost-control problem before it is a capability problem, and it has exactly one dangerous failure mode: the misroutes are quiet. Send a hard task to a small model and you do not get an exception; you get a fluent, plausible, wrong answer. Nobody files a bug titled "the classifier was optimistic today". The user just gets worse output and leaves.

So the non-negotiables, in order of importance:

  • Keep the eval suite as the arbiter. Routing decisions are only as good as the evals that grade them. If your evals are stale, your router is confidently stale too.
  • Human review stays in the loop for high-stakes outputs, at whatever sampling rate you can sustain. A spot-check habit beats a quarterly audit.
  • Log every routing decision, including the easy ones. When quality dips, you need to know whether the router got dumber, the model changed, or the traffic mix did.
  • Budget for the fallback. When the cheap model fails validation, escalate to the large model instead of shipping. The 200ms overhead is worth paying to avoid one bad customer-facing answer.

If you cannot say what your wrong-route rate is this week, you do not have a routing gateway; you have a cost lottery.

When routing is not worth it

Routing adds moving parts: a classifier to tune, policies to maintain, logs to read, evals to keep honest. It is not free, and it is not always worth it. Skip it when:

  • Traffic is low. If you send a handful of requests a day, the engineering time costs more than the flagship calls ever will.
  • It is a single-use internal tool. If one team uses it for one workflow, the variance in task complexity is probably tiny anyway.
  • It is a prototype. Prove the product works first. Add routing when the invoice proves the need, not before.
  • You cannot eval it. If you have no way to detect wrong answers, routing is just a way to fail at lower cost.

The rule I use: route when the request stream is heterogeneous, the volume justifies the machinery, and the eval suite can actually see quality differences. Everything else is optimization theater.

What I would tell you before you build this

Start with logging, not routing. Instrument every request with its true token cost for a few weeks and look at the distribution. You will find the cheap tier of traffic is bigger than you think, and that is your business case, grounded in your own data rather than my 65%.

Then build the classifier from three signals, not twelve: input length, task type, retrieval need. Add output structure once the first version is live. Resist adding signals because they seem clever; every signal is a maintenance burden with a failure mode.

Finally, wire the human review loop before the router goes to production. The review loop is what teaches the classifier what "hard" actually means in your domain. Without it, you are routing on generic assumptions about difficulty, and those are wrong in the ways that matter most.

I build this kind of system for teams: fixed scope from ₹25,000, fixed quote in writing, free 15-minute intro call. If your LLM bill is growing faster than your user base, that is a routing problem, not a model problem. That is my work.

essays.title: The 9-Step Pipeline That Turns a Repository Into a Reviewed PR
essays.excerpt: The 9-step pipeline that turns a repository into a reviewed PR: ingest, AST graph, graph-diff validation, load-aware assignment, and human review.
essays.body:
OnRamp is a repo-to-PR onboarding autopilot (live demo). You point it at a repository; it maps the codebase, classifies work, assigns it by role and load, opens one PR per issue with a coding agent, validates each PR by re-parsing it, and advances the linked task; merge approves the task and auto-closes the originating GitHub issue. This essay walks the 9 steps, spends the most room on the graph construction and the graph-diff validator, and ends with what broke and what is honestly unfinished. One rule frames everything: the agent proposes, humans dispose. Every PR is reviewed by a person; the agent does not merge.

Why onboarding is graph-shaped

Text search tells you where a string appears. It does not tell you what a class is for, who calls it, or what breaks when it changes. Onboarding fails when newcomers navigate by grep because the map is missing, and the map has to exist before the work can be split, assigned or verified. So the pipeline builds the map first and derives everything else from it.

The 9 steps, briefly

1. Ingest. Shallow clone plus changed-file detection. Cheap enough to run on every pass, and deliberately dumb: the expensive thinking happens on a parsed representation, not on raw files.

2. Graph. AST parse via Python's ast and tree-sitter across 20+ languages, in two passes. The first pass builds a dependency graph: imports, modules, files. The second pass builds an entity graph on top of it, with class, function and API-route nodes, and calls, inheritance, contains and serves edges. This is the heart of the system and the step most worth getting right. The second pass is what turns "these files reference each other" into "this route is served by this controller, which inherits from that base class and calls this service". Nodes carry kinds; edges carry semantics; everything downstream, from issue classification to validation, consumes this graph rather than re-deriving structure ad hoc.

3. Visualize. A standalone visualization.html with a D3 force-directed layout. Not decoration: reviewers use it to sanity-check the map before trusting any downstream automation, and a wrong map is easier to spot as a picture than as a JSON blob.

4. Query. Model-routed AI analysis. A multi-provider LLM router, free-tier-first, keeps cost sane and availability high; Redis exact and semantic response caching avoids paying twice for the same question on repeated runs.

5. Issues. Discovered work is classified by difficulty and assigned by role, so the right kind of contributor sees the right kind of task instead of a flat backlog.

6. Tasks. Load-aware assignment: the member with the fewest active non-terminal tasks wins, round-robin breaks ties, and overloaded members are skipped entirely. More on this below.

7. Solve. The coding agent opens one PR per issue with role-based labels. One issue, one PR; never a mega-PR that bundles unrelated work and defeats review. The 1:1 mapping between issue and PR is what makes the rest of the pipeline auditable.

8. Validate. The validator fetches the PR head branch, re-parses it, re-graphs it, and graph-diffs it against base: broken edges, new cycles. It then AI-verifies resolution and regressions with bounded retries, and writes a structured SENIOR_REVIEW.md. This step earns its own section below.

9. Advance. Opening the PR advances the linked task; merge approves it and auto-closes the originating GitHub issue. The board reflects reality because the board is wired to the version control system, not to someone's memory or a status field updated by hand.

The graph-diff validator

A diff tells you which lines changed. It does not tell you whether the change broke the architecture. The validator works in four moves: fetch the head branch, re-parse everything, rebuild the graph, and diff base against head. The graph-diff looks for edges that existed and now dangle (a call to something the PR deleted or renamed) and for cycles that did not exist before and now do. A PR that imports a removed module, or introduces a circular dependency nobody noticed, is caught structurally, not by hoping a reviewer spots it in a 400-line diff.

Why re-parsing beats trusting the diff or the agent's claim: the agent's own summary of its work is the one artifact you cannot trust, because the agent is optimizing for completion, not for honesty about what it broke. "It said tests pass" is not verification; a passing suite can coexist with broken structure the suite never covered. Re-deriving the graph from the pushed code is verification, because it does not depend on anyone's report, including the agent's. As the project puts it: a generated PR only counts once the validator re-parses it and diffs the graph, because the agent's own summary is the thing you cannot trust.

The AI-verify layer sits on top of the structural check, not instead of it: it reads the issue, the diff and the graph-diff output, and judges whether the original problem is actually resolved and whether anything regressed. Bounded retries matter here. The validator loops at most a fixed number of times, then escalates to a human with SENIOR_REVIEW.md in hand, instead of retrying forever and burning tokens on a task the agent cannot finish.

Load-aware assignment

The naive default is round-robin, and it distributes tickets evenly, which is not the same as distributing load. Your fastest closer accumulates the most active tasks under round-robin precisely because they finish quickly and pull the next one. Fewest-active-non-terminal-tasks-wins inverts this: assignment goes to whoever has the least in flight, round-robin only breaks ties, and members already over the threshold are skipped. The queue drains by capacity rather than by speed, and no single contributor becomes the accidental bottleneck the whole sprint routes through.

The subtlety is the non-terminal qualifier: finished work does not count against you, so a fast closer is not punished with a smaller queue once they deliver. You get rewarded with the next assignment only after your current plate clears, which is the behaviour you actually want.

How the pieces fail together

The pipeline is only as trustworthy as its weakest handoff, and the handoffs fail in instructive ways. A perfect graph feeding a hallucinating AI-verify step still ships bad merges; a rigorous validator fed an incomplete clone never sees the files that matter. The design response is defense in depth: structural checks before semantic ones, bounded retries before human escalation, one PR per issue so failures are scoped and attributable, and a human merge gate at the end whatever the automation says. When something slips through, the postmortem question is never "did the agent err" (it will, constantly) but "which layer should have caught this, and why did it not."

What broke

Noisy extraction on huge repos. tree-sitter and ast are accurate parsers, not accurate librarians. Generated code, vendored directories and polyglot build glue pollute the graph, and a graph polluted with junk is worse than no graph, because downstream agents trust it. The fix was aggressive scoping: ignore rules, generated-file detection, and an explicit acknowledgment that the entity graph is best-effort outside first-party code. On a huge monorepo you have to decide what the map is allowed to cover, or the map is unusable.

Agent self-reports passing validation. Early on, the AI-verify step occasionally rubber-stamped the agent's claim that "the change is safe". The agent is incentivized to declare victory; that is what completion looks like from the inside. The graph-diff did not care what the agent said. It compared structure against structure and flagged broken edges and new cycles regardless of narrative. That layer is what turned the system from an impressive demo into something a reviewer can actually rely on, and it is why validation is non-negotiable in the pipeline rather than an optional polish step.

What I would build next, and honest limits

Next: better monorepo support with mixed ownership, so the map can be scoped per team rather than per repo, and richer edge semantics, such as data-flow edges in addition to call edges, so the graph-diff can flag semantic breakage that preserves structural shape. Honest limits: entity extraction degrades on generated code; the AI-verify step can miss regressions that preserve graph topology; and the system proposes, it does not dispose. Every PR lands through human review and human merge. The 60+ merged PRs across 24 external repos in my own practice taught me the same lesson from the other side of the table: review is where quality is enforced, and no agent, however many passes it runs, removes it. The full breakdown is at the OnRamp case study.

essays.title: Building a Research Agent That Cites Its Sources
essays.excerpt: Building a research agent that cites its sources: plan, search, scrape, normalize, write, and why provenance is the product in RAG systems.
essays.body:
Everyone can generate a report now. The differentiator for a research agent is not whether the prose reads well; it is whether every sentence in that report can be traced back to a fetched source, with the URL attached. That is the hard part, and it is the part I spent most of my time on while building the ArchMind Research Agent, a Python, LangGraph and Streamlit system that plans a query, scrapes the web, normalizes what it finds and writes a cited brief. A report without verifiable citations is a confident rumor, and confident rumors are worse than no report at all, because they smuggle unverified claims into decisions.

The project and source: ArchMind Research Agent, code at github.com/KunjShah01/INTERNSHIP-ASSESSMENT. This is a build account, not a demo reel.

Why citation is the hard part, not generation

Generation is the solved half. Any competent model writes fluent paragraphs on demand. The unsolved half is grounding: for each claim the writer emits, there must exist a fetched document that supports it, and the system must attach that document's identity to the claim. Do this and you have a research tool. Skip it and you have a hallucination engine with a professional tone.

The architecture exists to serve exactly that constraint. The planner never lets the writer freelance; the writer never emits a claim without a source pointer; and the system is willing to say "not sourced" rather than smooth over a gap with plausible prose.

Architecture walkthrough: plan, search, scrape, normalize, write

Five stages, each with a contract and a failure mode. If any stage lies, the final report inherits the lie.

Plan: decompose before you retrieve

The planner breaks the request into sub-questions. This matters because broad questions retrieve broad, shallow junk. "What are the trade-offs of X" becomes three or four answerable sub-questions, each with its own retrieval pass. Contract: every sub-question must be individually answerable from sources; failure mode: sub-questions that are just rephrasings of the original vagueness, which means the planner has not actually reduced scope.

Search and scrape: fetch, do not imagine

Each sub-question triggers search, then scraping of the results worth reading. Contract: only fetched content enters the context; failure mode: the model reaching for parametric memory because the fetch failed and nobody noticed. I treat an empty scrape as a signal to widen or change the query, never as a cue to fill in from training data.

Extract: normalize the noisy web

Raw pages are unusable: nav bars, cookie walls, related-link farms, comment sections. The extractor applies readability-style extraction, deduplicates near-identical content across sources, scores sources for value, and drops the ones that will poison the report. Contract: output is clean, deduplicated, scored text with provenance metadata; failure mode: a JS-only shell page that passes extraction but contains nothing, or a login wall that yields a 200 status and zero content.

Write: grounded, cited, honest about gaps

The writer produces the report from retrieved evidence only, with each sourced statement carrying its URL. The report distinguishes what is sourced from what is inferred, and unverifiable claims get flagged, not smoothed over. Contract: no source, no claim; failure mode: a paragraph that starts as evidence and drifts into fluent speculation by its third sentence.

Attribution travels through the pipeline

One design decision that paid off: provenance metadata is attached at scrape time and never detached. The extractor does not just return clean text; it returns clean text with its source identity bound to it, and that binding survives the merge, the ranking and the write. The alternative, scraping first and re-attaching URLs later by matching sentences to pages, is where fabricated citations are born. If you cannot trace a sentence to a fetched document by construction, you will eventually cite a document that never contained the claim.

Taming noisy extraction

The web is predominantly noise. The extraction stage earns its keep by being picky:

  • Readability extraction to recover the article body from the chrome: navigation, sidebars, ads, footers, cookie banners.
  • Deduplication, because the same wire story republished across forty sites adds zero information and dilutes source diversity scores.
  • Source scoring to rank what deserves context space: primary sources and substantive analysis outrank listicles, SEO spam and content farms.
  • Hard drops for login-walled pages and JS-only shells that return markup without content. A 200 response tells you nothing about whether you got the thing.
  • Listicle and spam triage: "Top 10 X Tools You NEED in 2026" style pages are structurally designed to rank, not to inform; they go to the bottom or out.

None of this is glamorous. It is the difference between a RAG pipeline that cites real evidence and one that cites the SEO-optimized version of a rumor.

Drift on broad queries

Every research system degrades on broad queries, and mine was no exception. Ask for a wide-ranging landscape and retrieval starts returning everything and nothing: adjacent topics, marketing pages, outdated versions of the answer. The failure feels like success because the report still reads well.

The fix is decomposition, not more searching. Break the broad query into sub-questions, retrieve per sub-question, then merge with explicit conflict resolution: when sources disagree, the report says so and shows both. Tightening scope beats searching wider, every time. If the evidence is thin, the correct move is to narrow the question, not to lower the evidence bar.

I also found that broad queries expose citation rot fast: the top results are frequently stale rewrites of older content, so freshness and source scoring have to be part of retrieval, not an afterthought applied at write time.

Verification: quote-level grounding

Citation is only meaningful if a reader can check it. My verification pass works at the quote level: the writer's claims are mapped to supporting spans in the fetched sources, and the report marks what is sourced versus what is inferred. Claims that cannot be grounded are flagged explicitly rather than rephrased into confident vagueness.

Concretely, each claim in the output carries one of three states: sourced (a specific fetched span supports it), inferred (drawn from sourced material but not directly stated in it), or unverifiable (no support found). Only the first two are allowed in the final report body, and inferred claims are labelled as such. Unverifiable claims are either dropped or presented as open questions for the researcher, never as findings. This triage is what turns "cited" from a cosmetic footer of URLs into an actual guarantee.

It also changes how you debug. When a user disputes a line in the report, you do not re-read the whole document; you trace that line to its span. If the span is missing, the bug is in the writer. If the span is present but misread, the bug is in comprehension. If the span is present and correct but the reader was misled, the bug is in presentation. Each failure mode has a different fix, and quote-level mapping is what makes them distinguishable.

This is the uncomfortable feature: the agent will tell you when the web does not support an answer. That refusal is a feature. A research tool that never says "I could not verify this" is optimizing for user comfort, not for truth.

Limitations

This is an assistant for a researcher, not a replacement for judgment. Paywalled sources are invisible to it. Fast-moving topics can outrun retrieval: by the time a page is scraped and scored, the situation may have shifted. Citation rot is real: URLs die, content changes under the same URL, and a citation that resolved at write time may resolve differently later. JS-heavy and login-walled sources still slip through occasionally. And source scoring encodes my priors about what good sources look like, which is a bias, carefully applied but a bias nonetheless.

The right posture is: let the agent do the gathering, normalizing and first-draft synthesis, and let the human own the judgment calls, the disagreements between sources, and the final word on what to trust.

Two practical habits help if you operate the agent yourself. First, spot-check citations on a sample of reports, not just the ones that felt weak while reading; confidence and accuracy diverge exactly where the answer looks most polished. Second, keep a running list of sources that produced misleading or unusable output, and feed it back into source scoring. The extractor gets better when its misses are actually reviewed, which most teams never do.

The lesson that outlives the stack

Provenance is the product. Every other property, the Streamlit UI, the LangGraph orchestration, the scraping pipeline, exists to make the citations real. If you are building a research agent, decide on day one what happens when evidence is missing. My answer: flag it, never smooth it over. Everything else in the system is in service of that rule.

If you need a custom research agent grounded in your own corpus, or a RAG system whose citations hold up under scrutiny, that is my work. Fixed scope from ₹25,000, fixed quote in writing, free 15-minute intro call: https://kunjshah.in/contact.

essays.title: UPI Fraud Detection at a 0.01% Base Rate: Why Accuracy Is a Lie
essays.excerpt: UPI fraud detection at a 0.01% base rate: why accuracy is a lie, and the metrics, features and threshold-moving that actually catch fraud.
essays.body:
I built UPI Fraud Guard, a fraud scoring service for UPI-style transaction streams, with Scikit-Learn, XGBoost, Pandas and a Flask serving layer (source on GitHub). At the operating point I measured 88% detection rate, under 0.1% false positive rate, roughly 85% precision, and under 100ms inference. Every one of those numbers exists because of a decision I had to make explicitly, because at a 0.01% fraud base rate the naive defaults quietly betray you.

This essay is about the 0.01% problem: about one fraudulent transaction in ten thousand. Almost everything about fraud modeling at that rate is counterintuitive, starting with the metric everyone quotes first.

Why headline accuracy lies at extreme imbalance

At 0.01% prevalence, a model that predicts "never fraud" for every transaction is 99.99% accurate. It also catches nothing, and nobody would call it a fraud model. Yet accuracy is the first number most dashboards show, because accuracy is the one metric that never needs the base rate in the room to look good.

The failure mode is structural, not statistical. With 9,999 legitimate transactions for every fraud, the majority class dominates every aggregate you can compute. Gradient boosting will happily grind loss down by learning the majority pattern and treating the minority as rounding error unless you force the trade-off into the open: class weights, scale_pos_weight, or an explicit threshold decision after training. I used class weighting during training and then settled the real decision at the threshold stage, because that is where the business actually lives.

The honest way to read any fraud metric is to ask three questions before looking at the number. What is the base rate. What is the false positive count at the chosen operating point. What does a missed fraud cost. If the person presenting the model cannot answer those three, the model is not understood, only measured.

The metrics that matter here

Precision and recall at the operating point, not in the abstract. In this build, 88% detection rate means the model catches 88 of every 100 frauds shown to it; roughly 85% precision means about 15% of the alerts it raises are false alarms. Those two numbers are the same trade seen from two sides, and they move together whenever you move the threshold. Neither is "the" score; together they describe the operating point.

PR-AUC over ROC-AUC. ROC-AUC measures ranking quality across all thresholds, and the enormous mass of true negatives flattens the false positive axis so thoroughly that a near-useless model can still post a flattering number. The precision-recall curve has no true-negative axis to hide behind. At extreme imbalance, average precision is the honest summary of ranking quality, and it is the curve I would show a stakeholder first.

False positives per day, at your actual volume. A sub-0.1% false positive rate sounds tiny until you multiply it by real transaction volume. The unit the business feels is customers wrongly blocked per day, not percent false positive. I keep this qualitative on purpose: the right number depends on your traffic, and inventing one would be theater. What you can say firmly is that at 0.01% prevalence the legitimate majority is so large that even a very small false positive rate produces a large absolute number of wrongly blocked customers, which is exactly why precision at the operating point, not accuracy, deserves the attention.

Detection rate inside a false-positive budget. Set the false positive ceiling first (the maximum blocks your review team and your customers can absorb), then maximize detection within it. This framing makes the trade-off legible to people who do not read confusion matrices: here is the budget of friction we accept; here is the fraud we catch inside it.

Feature engineering that carried the model

The features that did the work were behavioral, not demographic:

  • Amount velocity. How much money moves, and how often, inside sliding windows. Fraudsters burn through freshly compromised instruments quickly; velocity windows catch the burst that any static amount threshold misses.
  • Merchant diversity. How many distinct merchants a user pays in a window. A sudden explosion in distinct payees is a classic account-takeover signature, and it is cheap to compute.
  • Geolocation entropy. How dispersed the locations behind the transactions are. Entropy turns where did this happen into how surprising is this scatter, which is the actual signal; a high-entropy burst from a normally tight pattern reads very differently from a routine travel week.
  • Time-of-day. Transaction timing against the user's own rhythm. Fraud scripts do not keep your hours.

Why counts beat demographics for fraud: demographics are stable and shared by millions of people, so they separate almost nothing. Behavioral counts are individual and hard to fake at speed. A fraudster can buy a new identity; they cannot cheaply manufacture a three-month velocity history that looks ordinary. This is also why XGBoost was a comfortable fit: gradient-boosted trees thrive on exactly this kind of tabular, count-and-ratio feature space, need no heavy preprocessing, and expose feature importances you can actually discuss with the people who own the review queue.

Threshold-moving instead of retraining

The 0.5 threshold is a convention, not a business decision. XGBoost outputs a score; the threshold converts scores into actions: allow, step-up verification, block, or route to review. Choosing that cutoff is the highest-leverage decision in the system, and it is free. No retraining, no new features, just a different place to act on the same ranking.

Pick the operating point by pricing the two errors. A missed fraud costs the fraud loss plus the dispute and chargeback process. A false block costs a good customer friction, a possible support contact, and a small but real risk of churn. When the cost of a miss outweighs the cost of a false block, lower the threshold; when the review queue is drowning in bad alerts, raise it. The procedure is mechanical: take a labeled validation slice, sweep the threshold, plot precision and recall against it, and mark the point where cost-weighted error is minimized. Then review that point with the people who absorb the consequences, not just with the model's author.

Threshold-moving also handles drift that retraining cannot. Fraud comes in waves; the base rate is not stationary. When prevalence shifts, the optimal cutoff shifts with it, and you can recalibrate on recent labeled data in an afternoon. Retraining is for when the relationship between features and fraud changes (new attack vectors, new flows, new instruments); threshold-moving is for when the prior changes. Conflating the two means retraining quarterly to fix what a calibration review fixes weekly.

Plain version: the model ranks; the threshold decides what to do with the ranking. You can disagree with the ranking, which is retraining and features, or you can disagree with the decision, which is the threshold. Most teams retrain when they are really just holding the wrong threshold.

What still fails

Novel attack patterns. The model is a statistical summary of past fraud. A genuinely new playbook has no support in the training data and will pass at high confidence. This is not a tuning problem; it is the boundary of supervised learning applied to adversaries who adapt.

Collusion rings. Individually ordinary accounts behaving in a coordinated ring look unremarkable per account while being anomalous jointly. Single-transaction scoring is blind to this by construction. You need graph features and ring-level review, which is a different system, not a patch on this one.

Legitimate-but-unusual behavior. Travel, a new phone, a one-off large purchase at 2am. The model cannot know these are you. Step-up verification, not silent blocks, is the right action for the uncertain middle, and it preserves the customer relationship while still checking the risky moment.

Drift monitoring is mandatory, not optional. Watch the alert rate, the precision on sampled manual review, and the score distribution over time. A silent base-rate shift or a new attack vector shows up there first. If nobody owns the monitoring, the model is decorative, not defensive.

Honest limits

The measured 88% detection rate means 12% of fraud gets through. That is the honest state of supervised fraud modeling at this base rate, and anyone selling you solved is selling you a demo. The under 100ms inference budget is the easy part; scoring a feature vector is cheap. The hard part is labels: fraud labels arrive late, partial and noisy, and every number in this essay inherits that noise. Systems that tell you otherwise are hiding their label pipeline.

If your fraud project quotes accuracy, ask for the confusion matrix at the chosen operating point, the false positives per day at your volume, and the drift monitoring plan. If those three answers are not ready, the model is not ready. The full write-up and the source are linked above; I would rather you read the limitations section than any marketing paragraph, including this one.
