essays.title: Shipping 152 Machine-Checked Pages: What Build-Time Guards Caught
essays.excerpt: Shipping 152 machine-checked pages: how Lattice uses build-time guards, a two-layer data model and 134 tests to keep an AI tools index honest.
essays.body:
Lattice is a curated, stack-ordered index of the 112 tools behind production AI systems, organized into 9 layers from inference and serving through routing, retrieval, fine-tuning, agent frameworks, orchestration, guardrails, prompts and evals, plus an off-stack learning section. It ships 112 per-tool pages, 6 head-to-head comparisons, 11 MDX essays, a Cmd-K palette, /compare and /all facets, feed.xml, llms.txt and sitemap.xml. All 152 routes are prerendered at build time and served as a Cloudflare Worker via OpenNext. There is no CMS, no runtime rendering, and no soft failure mode: the build is the editor. This essay is about what that discipline catches and what it costs. You can browse the result at lattice.kunjshah.in.

The premise: a directory is a database wearing a website costume

Most tool directories rot the same way. Someone adds an entry, nobody rechecks the licence, a comparison table quietly drifts, a broken link survives three redesigns, and a year later the site is a landfill with a nice search box. The entries were probably accurate on the day they were written. That is precisely the problem: accuracy at publish time is not accuracy, it is a snapshot, and snapshots decay.

The fix is not more editorial willpower or a quarterly reminder in someone's calendar. The fix is to treat the directory as structured data with invariants, put that data one build away from production with no editorial bypass, and make the build fail when the data lies. If a fact is worth publishing, it is worth asserting. Everything on the site is derived from the data model, and the build is the only path to production. The visual design is a costume; the database underneath is the product.

What the guards actually catch

Because the guards run on every build, the failures they catch never reach a reader, which makes them easy to underestimate. The classes are concrete: an entry added without a classification fails immediately instead of shipping as a mystery row; a comparison written against a tool that was renamed or dropped fails instead of rendering a lie; licence and cost fields past 6 months fail instead of aging silently into misinformation; a test regression in search ranking fails instead of degrading the one interaction every visitor uses. None of these are hypothetical risks; they are the default failure mode of every static reference site that relies on humans remembering to recheck facts. The guards convert "someone should probably re-verify this" into "the deploy is red until someone does."

The two-layer data model and the assertions that keep it honest

The data model splits what a tool IS from what it LINKS to. The IS layer is the classification: kind, deployment, licence, language, cost, useWhen, skipWhen, alternatives. The LINK layer is everything referential: URLs, docs, related toolings. An entry can be link-complete and still be a publishing error if its classification is missing or stale, because the classification is what makes the index navigable.

Three build-time assertions enforce the split:

  • A tool without classification throws. You cannot half-publish a tool. Missing kind, missing deployment shape, missing use/skip guidance: the build stops with the offending entry named.
  • A comparison naming an unknown tool throws. Head-to-head pages cannot reference phantoms, so a comparison can never render against a tool that does not exist in the index.
  • Licence or cost data older than 6 months fails the build. Staleness is not a warning in a log nobody reads; it is a hard stop in the only path to production.

These are deliberately unfriendly. A guard you can click through with an override flag is not a guard, it is a suggestion. Each assertion corresponds to a failure I actually want to be woken up for, and none of them allow partial success.

Staleness as a build failure

The 6-month rule for licence and cost data is the assertion I expect to annoy people most, including me. It means the site cannot quietly drift into confidently wrong information about what a tool costs or how it is licensed, which is exactly the information a reader is most likely to act on when choosing a stack. A wrong link is an inconvenience; a wrong licence or cost claim is a decision made on false premises.

The consequence is that maintenance becomes scheduled, not remembered. When the build fails, you refresh the data or you do not ship. There is no third option where the site deploys anyway and someone files a ticket. The cost is real: someone has to re-verify, and sometimes re-verification means a tool gets reclassified or dropped instead of updated. But the cost is paid in small, visible installments instead of one embarrassing launch of confidently wrong facts, and the failure message tells you exactly which entries need attention.

Static delivery as a feature

152 prerendered routes, no runtime rendering, no per-request server logic, served as a Cloudflare Worker via OpenNext, all built on Next.js 16, React 19, MDX and Tailwind v4. For reference content with zero personalization, this is the right architecture and not a compromise. Pages are invariant, so they are cacheable everywhere; there is no CMS to exploit or misconfigure, no preview environment leaking drafts, and no per-request failure mode between the reader and the page.

Adversarial traffic, which any public reference site eventually attracts, hits static assets and an edge worker, not an application with a database behind it. The attack surface is as small as a static file can make it. There is also an operational argument: no runtime means no runtime incidents, no connection pools, no cold-start tuning, no database migrations on a Tuesday.

The trade-offs are honest ones. No server-side personalization, by design; every page is the same for every reader. Content changes require a rebuild, measured in minutes, which is fine for reference material and wrong for a news feed. And the data pipeline must be sound, because there is no runtime net to catch bad inputs. That is precisely what the guards and tests exist for: they are the net, moved to build time where failures are cheap and loud.

What the 134 tests cover

The stack includes Vitest, and the 134 unit tests are pointed at the data, not at trivia. They cover four families of concern:

  • Data invariants. No orphan pages, so every tool is reachable from navigation and indexes; no unknown references, so comparisons, alternatives and cross-links all resolve to real entries; required classification fields present on every record.
  • Search ranking sanity. The Cmd-K palette ranks what it should. Regressions in scoring, tokenization or field weighting fail the suite rather than silently degrading the one interaction every user touches.
  • Frontmatter integrity. The 11 MDX essays carry the metadata the site assumes: titles, dates, categories, tags. Malformed frontmatter fails before it ever renders.
  • JSON-LD escaping. Structured data is a script context; unescaped content there is an injection risk, so escaping is tested explicitly instead of trusted.

The tests are invariants over trivia on purpose. I do not care whether a button has the right class name; I care whether the database underneath the site is internally consistent on every single build. That is the layer where reference sites actually fail in public, and it is the layer normal test suites skip because it is not component-shaped.

What it costs

The data model forces discipline on every tool you add. You do not get to publish "some LLM gateway thing" without committing to a kind, a deployment shape, a licence, a cost shape, and explicit use-when and skip-when guidance. Alternatives must exist in the index. If you cannot fill the classification honestly, the entry does not ship, and that is the correct outcome.

The guards are annoying on purpose. Adding a tool is slower than pasting a link into a CMS, and the friction is the feature: it is the difference between a directory and a dump. It also selects for contributors who can be precise, which shapes the whole corpus.

What you get in exchange is that content quality is a CI property, not an editorial hope. A green build means the reference is internally consistent, free of dangling references, and fresh within 6 months on the fields readers rely on most. The process is stricter than the output needs to look, which is exactly what you want from infrastructure nobody sees.

If you are building a reference site of your own, the transferable lesson is this: put your facts in a database, assert the invariants at build time, let staleness fail the deploy, and test the data, not the markup. The case study has the implementation details: Lattice on this site, or browse it at lattice.kunjshah.in.

essays.title: How to Hire an AI Engineer: A Technical Checklist for Founders
essays.excerpt: How to hire an AI engineer: five interview questions, the artifact test, paid trials and contract red flags, from an engineer who ships.
essays.body:
I sell AI engineering services from Ahmedabad, so read this with that bias in mind; it is also the checklist I would want on my desk if I were hiring. The relevant facts about my own practice: 17+ shipped systems, 60+ merged PRs across 24 external repos (OWASP, Microsoft AI-Engineering-Coach), 4 hackathon finals, and fixed-scope delivery with written scope, fixed INR price, code in your repo, and 40/60 payments. Every case study on this site carries a limitations section and a how-it-is-tested section. This essay is the buyer-side version of that honesty: how to screen an AI engineer without getting fooled by polish.

The wrong screen

Portfolio screenshots prove taste, not delivery. Dashboards with gradients and a plausible chart prove someone can arrange divs. Model names dropped in chat ("we use the latest frontier model") prove access to marketing, not judgment about when a smaller model wins. Certifications prove attendance; nobody has ever been saved by a badge. None of these show that the candidate can take a messy business problem, ship a system that survives contact with real users and real data, and then tell you the truth about what it cannot do.

The deeper problem with the wrong screen is that it selects for confidence. The candidates who perform best in a vibe interview are often the worst to hire, because an AI system fails quietly and a confident talker is never quiet. You are not hiring for enthusiasm; you are hiring for the engineer who will tell you your data is not ready before you pay to find out.

The right screen: five questions

Ask these five. Then listen for shape, not for story.

  1. Walk me through a production incident you caused and what you changed afterwards. Good answers are brief, concrete and owned: the system, the failure, the blast radius, the fix, the guardrail added afterwards. Red flags: a hero story where they single-handedly saved the company, or "I have never caused an incident in production", which means they have and did not notice or did not say.
  2. Show me the eval set for a system you shipped, and what fails below the floor. Good answers: they can describe or show the eval set, the pass threshold, the failure modes below the floor, and what they did about them. Red flags: no evals at all, or evals that only cover the happy path, or "we tested it manually and it worked well".
  3. What did your last system get wrong in production? Good answers: a specific, owned miss (a failure class, a drift, a bad assumption about inputs or users) and the change it forced. Red flags: blame the model, blame the data, blame the client, blame the requirements; never an owned miss.
  4. How do you verify an agent's work without trusting its summary? Good answers: re-derive verification from artifacts, re-run tests, re-parse outputs, diff structure, bound the retries, keep a human review gate. Red flags: "the agent said it passed". If they cannot explain verification independent of the agent's own report, they will ship you plausible output and call it done.
  5. What would you refuse to build for me, and why? Good answers: a real refusal with a reason (not measurable, not viable with the data available, not honest to ship, not worth the cost). Red flags: "nothing, whatever you need, I can build it", which is how you get a six-month boondoggle.

Good answers are brief, concrete and owned. Red flags are hero stories, missing evals, blame-the-model deflection, and an inability to name a single limitation of their own work. Notice that none of these questions can be answered by reading a landing page; they can only be answered by having done the work.

The artifact test

Before any contract, ask the finalist for a written one-page approach to your actual problem: what they would build, in what order, what they would measure, what they would not do yet, and what could make the whole thing fail. It costs them an hour; it reveals everything. You learn how they think under no pressure, whether they ask the right questions back, whether they understand the problem or merely pattern-match it to a previous project, and whether they can write plainly, which is the entire medium of every scope doc, status update and handoff note you will ever receive from them.

The artifact test also filters for the candidate who will tell you the truth in week one instead of week six. Vague artifacts produce vague projects. Sharp artifacts with explicit exclusions are the closest thing to a free sample of collaboration you will ever get.

Paid trial beats interview theater

A fixed-scope paid pilot is the highest-signal evaluation available, and it beats any interview format. The bands in my own practice: ₹15,000-35,000 for a workflow automation pilot, ₹25,000 and above for a product slice. Real work, real repo, real review, typically one to two weeks. You see commit quality, communication cadence, estimation honesty, and whether they finish what they scope. An interview shows you how someone talks; a pilot shows you how someone works, and only one of those ships your product.

Structure the pilot like a real engagement in miniature: written scope, definition of done, one revision round, fixed price. If they resist a paid pilot on principle, that is data. If they ask for it, that is data too.

Structure and incentives

Whatever the arrangement, the mechanics should look like this. A fixed quote in writing. 40% to start, 60% on delivery. Two revision rounds included. A definition of done written before any work begins. You own the code and the cloud account from day one, not after final payment. A handoff doc at the end covering architecture, env vars, failure modes, and how to operate the thing without them.

For reference, the commercial terms I work under: fixed-scope delivery from ₹25,000 for a 2-4 week engagement, ₹1,500 per hour for advisory, retainers of ₹30,000-75,000 per month for ongoing work, 40/60 payments, a free 15-minute intro call, and a fixed quote in writing. These terms exist because they force clarity on both sides. You cannot half-specify your needs and blame the delivery gap on the vendor, and the vendor cannot gold-plate the scope and bill for it. Friction at the contract stage is the cheapest place to find out whether both parties are serious.

Red flags in contracts and promises

  • Open-ended hourly with no cap and no definition of done. The incentive is inverted: the longer it takes, the more they earn. You need a cap, a scope, and a finish line.
  • "The AI will handle it" with no description of how the AI's output is verified, evaluated or reviewed by a human. Unverified AI output is a liability dressed as leverage.
  • No handoff doc, no test or eval story, no access for you to your own repo and cloud account. If you cannot operate the system without the vendor, you did not buy a system; you rented a dependency on a person.
  • Reluctance to put scope, price and timeline in writing. Verbal agreements dissolve exactly when they matter. Anything not written down will be renegotiated under stress, usually against you.
  • Promised outcomes without named assumptions. "Accuracy will be 95 percent" or "we will automate all of it", with no stated data assumptions, no eval set, no floor below which they will tell you to stop. Guaranteed outcomes without visible assumptions are marketing, not engineering.

Putting it together

The shape of a good hire process is short. Screen out the wrong signals. Ask the five questions. Read the artifact. Run a paid pilot. Sign a written scope with 40/60 and a definition of done. Then hold them to the same standard every case study on this site is held to: a limitations section and a how-it-is-tested section, written by the person who shipped the work. The honest ones will not blink at that request; the rest will negotiate, deflect, or disappear.

Even if you don't hire me, use this checklist; if you do, get in touch. And ask any candidate you shortlist to produce a limitations section and a how-it-is-tested section for their last project. The quality of that one-page answer will tell you more than any interview you have ever run.

essays.title: What You Learn Rebuilding BPE From Scratch (That tiktoken Hides)
essays.excerpt: What you learn rebuilding BPE from scratch that tiktoken hides: the merge loop, the GPT-2/4 regex, byte fallbacks, and a 15% token win on technical text.
essays.body:
I rebuilt the core of tiktoken in pure Python: MinBPE (source). It replicates tiktoken's core, uses the GPT-2/GPT-4 regex pre-tokenizer, byte-level encoding with byte fallbacks, and a custom vocabulary trained on technical corpora. Measured results: about 15% token reduction on technical text, roughly 50K merges learned into the vocabulary, and about 2x slower than tiktoken, which is the expected price of pure Python. This essay is about what building one teaches you that importing one hides.

Why build a tokenizer to use LLMs

Most "the model is stupid" reports are tokenization artifacts: split identifiers, inconsistent casing, invisible characters, numbers chunked unhelpfully, a stray non-breaking space that changes the entire token stream. Once you have written a tokenizer, you can spot these because you have had to decide where every byte goes. Building one is the cheapest debugging education available in the LLM stack, and it pays for itself the first time a weird output turns out to be an encoding problem rather than a reasoning problem.

There is a second reason, less discussed: cost. You pay per token, and tokens are produced by a deterministic algorithm you can inspect. Knowing the algorithm means knowing why two prompts with identical word counts differ in price, why a pasted stack trace balloons, and why minified JSON is cheaper than pretty-printed JSON. tiktoken gives you the count; writing BPE gives you the count and the reasons.

The algorithm in plain terms

Byte Pair Encoding starts from bytes. Every byte value is a token, so your initial vocabulary is 256 entries and nothing is ever unknown. Count adjacent token pairs across the corpus, merge the most frequent pair into a new token, append it to the vocabulary, and repeat. After roughly 50K merges, frequent byte sequences (whole common words, ubiquitous subwords, common operator pairs in code) are single tokens, and the vocabulary is a compressed record of what the corpus says most often.

The vocab IS the algorithm. There is no separate model underneath; the merge list is the compression. Encoding a fresh string replays the merge list in the order the merges were learned; decoding reverses the expansion by substituting each merged token with its two children recursively. If you understand counting pairs and merging the winner, you understand the entire machine. Everything else is engineering around that core: efficient pair counting, caching, memory layout, and the pre-tokenizer in front.

One property follows directly and is worth internalizing: the vocabulary is greedy and local. Each merge is the best available compression step at the time it was made, not a global optimum. That is why the merge order matters and why replaying merges in the wrong order produces garbage. The tokenizer is an ordered procedure, not a lookup table, and treating it as a lookup table is the first misconception people bring to the exercise.

The GPT-2/4 regex pre-tokenization

Before merging begins, the text is split with the GPT-2/GPT-4 regex into chunks: roughly, contractions, runs of letters, numbers, punctuation with optional leading space, and runs of whitespace. This matters because merging across chunk boundaries would fuse halves of unrelated words into single tokens, which is compression in name but garbage in effect. The regex enforces that merges happen inside linguistically sane units.

The regex does more work than people expect. It is why "hello world" and "helloworld" tokenize differently, why a leading space changes the token stream, and why the same word can cost a different number of tokens depending on what precedes it. Contractions like "don't" get split into a letter-run and an apostrophe-run rather than one blob, which keeps apostrophe handling uniform across thousands of words. If a prompt's price or behavior changed when you rephrased one sentence, the pre-tokenizer is usually the reason, and now you know where to look.

Byte fallbacks

Because the base vocabulary is bytes, any byte sequence encodes. There is no unrepresentable input, ever: an emoji, a rare script, a corrupted download; all of it round-trips through the vocabulary. The cost is ugly splits on characters the corpus never showed. A rare glyph can shatter into several byte tokens, inflating sequence length and occasionally garbling generation on low-resource scripts. Byte fallback is a correctness guarantee, not an aesthetic one: nothing is ever impossible to encode, but nothing is promised to be cheap, either.

This is also why tokenizers trained predominantly on English-heavy corpora are measurably more expensive per sentence in other languages: bytes for unfamiliar scripts merge poorly, and you pay in length what the vocabulary never learned to compress. Script diversity in training data is not an ethics add-on; it is compression economics.

What a technical-corpus vocab buys

A vocabulary trained on technical corpora learns merges for the strings that dominate that text: identifiers, imports, common API names, ML and systems terminology. Domain terms become single tokens, so the same technical content fits into fewer tokens; I measured about 15% token reduction on technical text. That is directly cheaper calls and denser effective context, bought by no longer re-spelling the vocabulary of your domain one fragment at a time.

The catch is obvious and honest: a specialist vocabulary is worse on general text. It will mishandle content outside its corpus, and you will not notice until the bill or the quality regression shows up. Specialization is a bet on the workload, and it pays exactly when the workload is real. If your traffic is 80% code and ML prose, the bet is rational; if it is half customer support, keep the general tokenizer.

What it taught about LLM behavior

Token boundaries explain more mysterious model behavior than any other single concept I know:

  • Long identifiers. A 40-character snake_case name fragments into chunks the model sees unevenly. The model does not see the identifier; it sees shards, which is why exact recall of long identifiers, hashes and UUIDs is unreliable no matter how good the underlying model is. If you need exact reproduction of opaque strings, put them in the prompt verbatim and keep them short, or do not expect verbatim recall.
  • "Strawberry" counts fail. Character-level questions ask the model to count letters inside tokens it never encountered as letters. The r-r-r in "strawberry" may live inside one or two tokens, invisible to the model as a sequence of characters. Asking about letters is asking about an abstraction the model was never given, and no amount of reasoning fixes a missing layer.
  • Leading spaces change meaning. " world" and "world" are different tokens with different embeddings. Prompts, code blocks and chat templates are sensitive to exact spacing for this reason, and template designers know it; inconsistent indentation in few-shot examples is not cosmetic.
  • Numbers chunk strangely. Digits group into tokens of varying widths depending on position and locale conventions, which is one reason arithmetic on multi-digit numbers is shakier than arithmetic on single digits, and why digit-heavy tasks reward careful prompting.

The build itself, honestly scoped

The project is deliberately small enough to hold in your head: a pure Python trainer that counts adjacent pairs over a corpus, a merge loop that emits an ordered merge list, and encoders and decoders that replay it. The pre-tokenizer is the GPT-2/GPT-4 regex, not a hand-rolled approximation, because approximating it teaches you nothing and breaks parity with the reference implementation. The vocabulary was trained on technical corpora, which is where the 15% token reduction on technical text comes from, and the merge list landed at roughly 50K entries. Everything in the repo is inspectable; nothing is hidden behind a compiled extension or a training-framework dependency.

Honest trade-offs

This implementation is about 2x slower than tiktoken. It is pure Python and it shows; production tokenizers are Rust or Go for a reason, because tokenization sits on the critical path of every request in a high-throughput system. The exercise pays for itself in debugging time and in cost intuition, not in serving speed, and nothing here should be deployed where tokenizer latency matters. Build it to understand it; ship the fast one. The case study with the full write-up is at MinBPE on this site; the code is at TOKENIZER-FROM-SCRATCH.
